t: Research Bite #71: Marked Pedagogies: Examining Linguistic Biases in Personalized Automated Writing Feedback
q: This study tested whether large language models change their writing feedback based on who they think a student is.

The researchers took 600 American eighth-grade persuasive essays from the public PERSUADE dataset and asked four widely used models (GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-turbo, and two Llama models) to give feedback, varying only the student attributes named in the prompt: race, gender, motivation, and learning needs such as English language learner or learning disability status.
The essay text never changed. Comparing the language across conditions, they found systematic, stereotype-aligned shifts.

Feedback for students marked by race, language, or disability tended towards more praise, less substantive critique, and assumptions of limited ability, focusing on surface corrections rather than ideas. The authors call these patterns 'Marked Pedagogies.'

AI writing tools don't treat every student the same. Tell a model that a student is low-achieving, an English language learner, or from a particular racial group, and its feedback shifts in stereotyped ways: more praise, less substantive critique, even when the writing is word-for-word identical.

t: Why Your Best Failure Story Matters More Than Your Wins
q: In this live, I was joined by Elina , who writes the Leadership Capability System on Substack, to discuss our article on how to build trust when things go wrong . The premise we started from is that almost all of us are coached, formally or informally, on how to present a win, yet hardly anyone is taught how to talk about a miss.

The instinct is either to hide or to rush in and explain, and the argument we make is that two stages of work need to take place before you open your mouth. There is the factual side, collecting the data and understanding the scale and root cause, and the emotional side, understanding what the miss has stirred up in you.

The same miss does not warrant the same conversation with everyone, so this stage is about who needs to know, what matters to them, which format fits, who else is in the room, and how much trust you already have in the bank. Narrate is the actual talking, and we offered a structure for it called FOCUS (Framing, Observation, Context, Understanding and Solution), which mirrors how people naturally want to receive difficult news.

I offered the two framings to avoid, the victim frame ("they rejected my report") and self-flagellation ("I misjudged the brief, I'm terrible"), both of which leave the failure as the headline, against the one that worked: the analysis is solid and gives us the raw material, what it doesn't yet do is serve your communications objective, so the next version will build it around the message you want to carry. Follow up is what makes the trust genuinely rebuild rather than just patching the moment.

It covers the full four-stage protocol (Process, Prepare, Narrate, Follow up), the FOCUS structure with a before-and-after worked example, a ready-to-use AI prompt that reframes your draft and flags the gaps before you send, and a Harder Cases section. You can get it below; it's free for paid subscribers , and the price of a coffee for everyone else.

The through line is that a miss is rarely the thing that damages you. What damages you is walking in with your emotions first, talking to the wrong person, or handing over a problem with no plan attached.

t: Why You Cannot Believe Your Way Into Learning
q: For most people, the hardest thing to understand about learning is that the strategies which work in the short term often feel like failure, while the ones that pay off in the future often feel like success in the present. A new paper in Educational Psychology Review applies this uncomfortable truth to the most popular intervention in modern education, growth mindset, and finds it wanting: as a standalone treatment it produces effects on achievement that are vanishingly small and disappear entirely under proper scrutiny.

It is short, intuitive, cheap, and almost too good to be true; an intervention can be delivered in as little as ten minutes through an online module, and it leaves both teacher and pupil feeling that something transformative has occurred. In a new paper, Anne Cleary and Daniel Robinson place it alongside learning styles and grit, in a small family of concepts that are quick to grasp, relatively easy to administer, and almost entirely resistant to disconfirmation or falsification.

The for-profit programme Brainology was marketed to schools as an effective intervention, priced at several thousand dollars per school per year; and then, in 2015, the Institute of Education Sciences awarded a multi-million-dollar grant to investigate whether it actually worked. Cleary and Robinson give a great analogy; a pharmaceutical company selling a drug to patients first, and securing funding for the trial afterwards.

Robert Bjork's phrase for the useful kind of struggle, the desirable difficulty , captures the whole problem in two words: the desirable thing is, by design, difficult, and the difficult thing is often hidden. It is a feel-good method in a field where the things that feel good rarely work and the things that work rarely feel good.
This is not motivation in the familiar sense; it is honesty about the structure of learning. A slogan that tells children how easy initial learning ought to feel is simply dishonest.

He presents this as a defence of mindset, but it is closer to a concession I think, because it grants the structural point precisely: belief is inert without a vehicle to carry it. Yeager argues that the near-zero averages in the meta-analyses are misleading, an artefact of pooling the contexts in which the effect is real with the many in which it is absent; the effects are heterogeneous, they argue, not absent.

I think the negative attitudes to her work as more a result of lethal mutations of growth mindset rather than the work itself. In fact Paul Kirschner and I dedicated a chapter to it in our book How Learning Happens .

t: Why We Jump to Conclusions About What Works in Education
q: The most visible explanation is not always the most important one. Have you ever noticed how quickly we create explanations for things we observe?

Before concluding that one factor caused an improvement, we need to ask what else may have contributed, and whether the available evidence actually supports the claim. This is precisely why educational researchers rely on carefully designed studies rather than intuition alone.

Linking Halton's success to a particular teaching method is not as clear-cut as the article suggests. Why this explanation is more complicated than it first appears The central problem in the Globe's article is the leap from correlation to causation.
The following year, Ontario increased from 54 per cent to 58 per cent while Halton increased from 70 per cent to 74 per cent. The Grade 3 and Grade 6 mathematics scores show similar patterns.

It closely resembles Building Thinking Classrooms (BTC), a framework adopted by many schools and school boards across Ontario. If this approach were responsible for Halton's gains, we might expect superior outcomes in all boards where it has been implemented.

As the cognitive scientist Barak Rosenshine documents in his widely cited American Educator article , successful lessons typically combine multiple instructional approaches, including whole-class instruction, modelling, guided practice, questioning, and independent practice. Rather than asking whether teachers should lecture or facilitate, a more useful question is when and how different instructional strategies are most effective.

Before concluding that one "different" teaching method explains a school board's success, we should demand evidence capable of separating instructional effects from the many other influences on student achievement. Inferring causation from correlation is a particularly risky habit in education reporting, because the policy stakes are simply too high.

t: Why Leaders Must Withhold Judgment to Unlock Team Creativity
q: It turns out the sequence in which evaluation enters the creative process is not a minor procedural detail. Deciding when evaluation enters is among the most consequential choices a leader makes when trying to unlock a team's creative potential.

Critical thinking and rigorous evaluation are essential for producing practical, impactful solutions for most problems and opportunities. Research consistently confirms that judgment and critique, however well-intentioned, carry a hidden cost when introduced too early.

Judgment during the ideation phase has been shown to suppress creativity by narrowing attention before enough proposals and options have been generated. When a leader signals, even subtly, that ideas will be assessed as they emerge, team members shift from generative to defensive thinking, restricting the field of possibilities before it has a chance to expand.

The evidence supporting this principle dates all the way back to the 1950s, when brainstorming expert and advertising executive Alex Osborn proposed that suspending judgment during ideation is crucial for generating a wide range of creative ideas. Osborn insisted that criticism be banned during the idea-generation phase, creating a safe space for unusual ideas to surface.
That logic has since been validated across decades of research. The practical implication for leaders is a discipline of deliberate sequencing.

Divergent thinking must come first and convergent evaluation second. Good leaders create the conditions in which people can brainstorm, experiment, and build on successful approaches without the fear of judgment.
When people feel safe to generate novel ideas, creativity follows. The most creative teams are not always those filled with highly imaginative people.

t: There's More to the Mental Health Crisis Than Smartphones and Social
q: View this post on the web at In the past few years, parents and teachers have become acutely aware of the risks of smartphones and social media to young people. I'm glad to see schools banning smartphones; I was thrilled to see Australia set 16 as the minimum age for social media and I hope many countries will follow that lead.

But protecting kids digitally isn't enough to protect them emotionally. Hot off the presses: Psychologists analyzed 307 studies of nearly 83,000 students over 35 years across the U.S., U.K., and Canada.
It turns out that perfectionism has been accelerating over time. Young adults feel growing pressure to be flawless--and it started a generation before smartphones and social media.
The spike is especially pronounced for concerns about making mistakes and being seen negatively by others. And this fear of judgment is a significant risk factor for anxiety and depression.
Modern technology may be an amplifier, but it isn't the root cause. Perfectionism stems from unreasonably demanding expectations and unduly harsh criticism.

It's stoked by the parents who punish their kids for getting an A-, the teachers who embarrass their students for getting a math problem wrong, and the coaches who berate their athletes for missing a shot. To counter perfectionism, here are some basic messages that parents, teachers, and coaches can reinforce: 1.

t: The Things We Never Say
q: Elizabeth Strout's most recent novel The Things We Never Say deals with openness and secrecy in relationships, and the difficulty of talking about what's going on between people, even when we long to. In the novel the central character, Artie Dam, complains to his wife that at the neighbourhood cocktail parties they attend together, people aren't having 'real' conversations.

Moreover, Artie finds out that the new friend he can open up to has just voted for Trump to be president for the second time, a prospect which Artie views with complete horror. They can talk together about their relationships, unusual in men of their age, but they don't talk about politics.

The closer the relationship, the higher the emotional stakes, but in every relationship there are comprises, silencings and negotiation with ourselves and with others . This is not to say that the opposite of idealisation is true, that we shouldn't be open with each other, and should avoid discussing the uncomfortable, but that to rub along with each other requires the exercise of practical judgement and a constant wrestling with what to conceal and what to reveal, caught up in the tensile, fluctuating dialectic of trust.

But that's not how it feels to many people for whom eligibility criteria, KPIs, outcomes, pathways, packages of care might sound like meaningless bureaucratic jargon. They know what relational public services feel like when they experience them, and certainly when they don't.

From the presentations I heard, there were a number of cases where citizens had not been asked systematically about what mattered to them, or if they had been, public services were unable to respond flexibly and adaptively. But entering into 'real' conversations was often the start of a process which often provoked strong emotions on all sides.

One was entitled What if Learning Isn't the Problem, presented by Karen MacNeil of the Phronesis Partnership and Pauline Lunn (In Control Scotland), which, amongst other things, was a highly relational account of institutional power politics. No surprise that Karen would tell me that 'everything is political', and that the project involved phronesis (nominative determinism for Karen's organisation), the entanglement of practical judgement, politics and ethics.

Collaborating better also involved coming to terms with how everyone was contributing to a less helpful dynamic, including oneself, potentially othering different teams as being the guilty party. The French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu confessed to being much more interested in why things stay the same, rather than why they change.
x: Talking about what's going on means making things visible which perhaps we would rather remain invisible.

t: A Lethal Mutation of Servant Leadership
q: If you're reading this as an educator, I'm interested in your experience of last school year. I'm interested in what the poll will find as normal, since in my experience, these kinds of burnout behaviors are ubiquitous among educators.

William Jones defines lethal mutation as "an idea or a practice that is prompted by sound scientific evidence, but is implemented in a way that reduces, or even completely negates, its effectiveness." Just as our profession is facing a profound crisis of teacher burnout and attrition, we're also facing the same dual crises in our school leaders. Now, I'm not saying that the primary cause of the educator burnout crisis is this mindset.

q: One of the more frustrating experiences for leaders occurs when a team member becomes so fixated on financial incentives that they interpret everything through the prism of compensation. These team members have an unusual obsession with financial rewards that makes them difficult to satisfy.

But they strongly believe even good citizenship should come with a financial reward. They typically make it very well known that they are not paid fairly for what they do, and consistently ask for increases in compensation, especially as their job or role expands in any way.

They are commonly taught by parents, role models, and prior leaders to place an extreme value on financial achievement. The lesson they learn, sometimes very early on, is to view nearly all workplace activities through a cost-benefit lens.
They can become highly argumentative over the smallest financial issue or payout. Interestingly, the research shows that increases in financial incentives do not typically improve performance.

Traditional economic thinking assumes that if a leader pays people more, they'll perform better. Research in psychology and behavioral economics has shown this is true only for simple, repetitive, or mechanical tasks.

That's because most people are motivated by more than financial outcomes. Research confirms that performance improves most when compensation is fair, the performer is given the autonomy over how the work is done, and they believe in a higher purpose that makes it matter.

Naturally, leaders must weigh their approach against the many specific facts that surround the team member, including how talented they are, how unpopular they have become, and how annoying their dissatisfaction is. But at some point, many coin-operated team members wear out their welcome.

q: For most people, the hardest thing to understand about learning is that the strategies which work in the short term often feel like failure, while the ones that pay off in the future often feel like success in the present. t: The Need to Separate Criticism From Authority
q: One of the most dangerous things a leader can do is make it hard for people to tell them the truth. Most leaders don't intend this, but through subtle reactions to criticism, defensive rebuttals, and a quiet withdrawal of favor, they teach people that honesty carries a cost.

To counter this, good leaders design feedback processes that separate criticism from authority. This means deliberately severing the link between who gives feedback and who decides what to do with it.

People below with good ideas and sharp observations learn to censor themselves. They don't offer criticism or raise new ideas because experience has taught them that their views aren't fully welcome or valued.
Those without authority get to offer a full critique of what they see and what would make it better. Those above receive the benefit of their insights without the obligation to respond or defend.

The Braintrust works like this: At regular intervals during a film's production, the director screens the current cut for a small group of trusted colleagues and peers, including writers, storytellers, and fellow directors. The director weighs the criticisms against their own instincts and decides.

t: Stop Pretending Novices Are Little Experts
q: One of the most robust findings to emerge from cognitive science is that experts and novices do not think in the same way. This difference is not simply a matter of experts knowing more facts or possessing greater intelligence. Rather, experts have developed extensive, well-organized networks of domain-specific knowledge that fundamentally alter how they process information, solve problems, and make decisions.

Many of the most celebrated student-centered approaches seem to rest on assumptions that are difficult to reconcile with what cognitive science tells us about how expertise develops. While these approaches are often praised for increasing activity, engagement, collaboration, and student ownership, they frequently place students in situations that require forms of thinking that are characteristic of experts rather than novices.

The student in a jigsaw activity is not an expert. The student is a novice who has had a brief encounter with new information. Yet the structure of the activity assumes that this novice is capable of performing tasks that are normally associated with expertise. The result is that students often find themselves struggling not only to learn the material but also to teach it simultaneously.

Advocates of student-centered learning often point to the level of activity taking place during these lessons as evidence of their effectiveness. Students are talking. Students are moving. Students are collaborating. The classroom appears intellectually vibrant. Yet visible activity is not the same thing as learning.

Many student-centered instructional approaches invert this relationship. Rather than helping students acquire the knowledge that makes expert thinking possible, they often assume that placing students in expert-like roles will somehow produce expert-like knowledge and thinking. Cognitive science suggests the opposite.

The ability to think critically, solve problems, and reason effectively is heavily dependent upon what one already knows. Instructional designs that ignore this sequence deprive students of both the knowledge and the thinking the lesson was meant to produce.

t: Steal the Principle, Not the Playbook
q: When Phil Jackson won eleven NBA championships using the triangle offense, thousands of basketball coaches rushed to install it and failed.
Solutions, even grand ones, rarely travel well. They are context-specific and produce great outcomes because of the unique mix of ingredients present at that moment.

The triangle offense worked well for Jackson because he had Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen, players of rare basketball intelligence who could improvise within the structure and share decisions on the fly to keep defenders off-balance. Give the same system to a roster without that instinct, and it doesn't underperform. It collapses.

When Atul Gawande studied aviation checklists and applied the idea to surgery, he did not import them into the operating room. He asked what principle made them work and then built a new tool for a new context — the surgical checklist. The result was one of the most consequential patient safety interventions in modern medicine.

Leaders who learn the most from studying others treat every success story as a puzzle to reverse engineer, not a photocopy to reproduce. They don't ask, 'What did they do?' Instead, they ask, 'Why did it work there?'

q: Ross Wiener's op-ed struck me as oddly incurious about why achievement scores rose during the No Child Left Behind era and why scores declined when it ended.

t: Coaching and the Freedom to Be Yourself
q: The popularity of coaching reflects its value. The 'scaling,' has split coaching into two different things at the extremes. On one end, AI-enabled 'coaching' tools now offer employees company-wide something like human optimization — stripping out the relationship and honing in on what to do and how to do it.

Here is the current state of coaching: it spans the space between human workforce optimization (with or without human intervention) and genuine human transformation. Which is better for people is the one that gives them more power and more choice; that is the latter — transformational coaching in relationship with real humans.

The last fifty years have seen psychotherapy become the dominant socio-emotional framework for self-understanding in the Western world. When we locate the source of our struggles primarily in our stories of distress and difference, we frame what might otherwise be individuality — intensity, sensitivity, unconventional thinking — as pathology.

Transformational coaching is countercultural in a good way. Our world trains compliance, submission, and passivity from a young age, moving us away from independent thinking and realizing our own uniqueness.

Transformational coaching stands in contrast to three powerful social forces that push us toward conformity: the ubiquity of the therapeutic model of who we are, work that is increasingly alienating, and a social reality that leaves us isolated.

t: 626: Great Leaders Are Willing to Disappoint the Wrong Customers
q: Your business lives or dies on one decision your customers make without you in the room. They choose you, or they choose someone else. When nothing about your offering helps that choice in your favor, you do not lose in a single dramatic moment. You fade. You become irrelevant.

A new segment opens, so you chase it. A competitor adds a feature, so you match it. A loud prospect wants something outside your lane, so you build it. Each move feels reasonable on its own. Strung together over a few years, they sand down every edge that once made you worth choosing.
To own a place in the customer's mind, you have to be willing to give something up. The leaders who cannot bring themselves to disappoint anyone end up memorable to no one.

Get this right, and your focus hardens into something rivals struggle to copy. A clear position points every decision in the same direction, and that consistency is exactly what makes it hard to imitate.

q: Sometimes we are so busy doing good things that we forget to ask what our actions are actually creating. We attend the meeting, send the email, make the plan, launch the program. We respond to the request, add the appointment, finish the task, take the call, move the project forward.

t: We've Been Studying System 1 All Along
q: Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken, and very bright. She majored in philosophy. As a student, she was deeply concerned with issues of discrimination and social justice, and also participated in anti-nuclear demonstrations. 85% to 90% of participants chose Option B. The probability of two events occurring together can never be greater than the probability of one of the events occurring alone. The Linda Problem shows that people do not reason directly from information; we reason from the meaning we construct from that information.

t: The Old Me Still Answers the Phone First

t: The Mystery Illness That Explains What We Keep Getting Wrong About Kids
q: At first, the doctors saw the skin. That was the thing nobody could ignore. South Carolina children were showing up with strange, painful rashes on their hands, arms, necks, and faces, especially where the sun touched them.

The doctors looked for contagion. They inspected buildings, bedding, water, air, routines. A mysterious illness moving through orphanages, prisons, asylums, mill villages, and poor Southern communities was spreading, and no one could figure out why.

I think we are staring at visible symptoms and mistaking them for the problem. Teachers see children melting down over small frustrations. Parents see children unable to tolerate boredom. Pediatricians and therapists see anxiety, dysregulation, and emotional fragility.

We call it behavior. Defiance. Attention-seeking. Anxiety. Poor executive function. Weak social skills. Lack of motivation. Immaturity. Those descriptions are not necessarily wrong. A rash really is a rash. A meltdown really is a meltdown. The question is whether we are looking deeply enough.

t: People Often Resist a Decision Solely Because of How It Was Made
q: Decades of research in organizational psychology point to a consistent and humbling finding: How a decision is made matters as much as what was decided — and sometimes more. The quality of a decision is often secondary to the decision process.

When people feel they were heard before a decision was finalized, given a genuine opportunity to voice concerns, and treated with respect throughout the process, they are far more willing to accept and support the result, especially when they dislike it or it directly disadvantages them.

When people feel excluded, rushed through, or simply informed after the fact, they resist the decision. This resistance is not always vocal or openly expressed in advocacy. It shows up as disengagement, quiet non-compliance, backroom complaints, and poor execution.

Research has consistently shown that people distinguish clearly between having a voice and having a vote. They do not expect to influence every decision, but they want to be genuinely considered before one is made.

All organizations run on discretionary effort. Whether team members go beyond the minimum, support initiatives they did not choose, and trust leaders through uncertainty depends more on the decision process than many leaders realize.
The bottom line is this: Leaders who remember that the decision process is the message get more done.

t: Leadership
q: Leaders are in the business of helping those who report to them. Whenever a team member hits a wall, leaders are there to lend a hand. The problem could be a stalled project, a skill gap, a failing relationship, or a situation too delicate to navigate alone.

How they help comes down to a deceptively simple choice: when offering support, leaders can "go high" or they can "go low." Going high means elevating the solution above both the leader and the team member. As the metaphor implies, the leader goes above the situation to survey the broader landscape, spots what is needed, and pulls it in.

Going low means the leader descends into the work alongside the team member. They pull up a chair, roll up their sleeves, and work through the problem together. Imagine a new sales rep who can't crack a difficult client conversation.

The leader sits on the next call, debriefs in real time, and coaches from inside the problem. Going high preserves the leader's time, builds the team member's network, and creates independence. Going low builds trust, transfers knowledge directly, and is often the only way to solve the problem quickly.

Go high too often, and you are likely a hands-off manager who only leads when called upon. Go low as a default, and you are likely a micro-manager who gets into the weeds on everything, and not just when asked. The wrong instinct is to always default to one or the other.

The right question isn't "Which approach is better?" It's "Which approach best fits the situation?" To make that call, leaders should consider three factors: urgency, capability gap, and growth stage. If this is a common problem that Page 1 others have faced, go high. If the team member is early in their development and needs attention, go low.

What the Hawthorne Effect Really Is The Hawthorne Effect traces back to a series of experiments conducted in the 1920s and 1930s at the Hawthorne Works, a Western Electric factory near Chicago. Researchers set out to study whether changes in physical working conditions, such as lighting levels, break schedules, working hours, etc. Productivity improved almost regardless of what change they made.

The results were consistently positive, no matter the direction of the change. The conclusion researchers eventually Page 1 drew was striking: it wasn't the changes themselves that were driving the improvement. It was the fact that workers knew they were being observed.

The Hawthorne Effect, in its simplest form, is this: people change their behavior when they know they are being watched. I do want to note that subsequent researchers have debated the original findings and their interpretation, and the data from those studies was messier than the clean narrative suggests. But the core behavioral insight has helped up over the decades of organizational research and real-world leadership experience: attention shapes behavior.

If I think my child is simply being difficult, I tighten control. If I think my child may be under-practiced, I start looking for the missing practice field.

Modern children often have less free play, less neighborhood life, less outdoor time, less boredom, less responsibility, less mixed-age peer culture, less movement, less manageable risk, less community, and fewer chances to solve ordinary problems without adults immediately smoothing the road.

t: An AI Marking Case Study: From Four Hours to Twenty Minutes
q: Adding in the AI makes it possible for just one teacher to complete all the required human judging.

People quite rightly worry that AI assessment means teachers stop engaging with student writing, and that this could have a knock-on effect on student engagement. Why bother working hard on a piece of writing when your teachers can't be bothered to read it? But in the system we have designed, every script is seen twice by a human, which is double what happens with traditional non-AI rubric based assessment.
While judging, teachers can click a microphone button and speak their feedback. The AI transcribes what they say, polishes it and turns it into a written comment in student friendly language.

That is incredibly rapid. I used to be a secondary English teacher, and using traditional marking, I would estimate that it would take me at least four hours, maybe more, to produce this level of quality personalised feedback and reliable scores.
The audio feedback is not AI feedback, it is human feedback and it shows the student that the teacher has read their work. But because speaking is much faster than typing, it is much more efficient.

t: Work Whiplash
q: Nothing burns great people out faster than what I call work whiplash. People can handle hard work. They struggle when priorities constantly reverse, decisions get made and un-made, and goals keep changing underneath them.

One of the most demoralizing things that can happen to someone at work is spending weeks pushing something uphill only to find out the strategy changed, the project no longer matters, or another team was quietly working on the same thing on the other side of the building.

I think leaders often underestimate how emotionally exhausting this is for their teams. You are holding context that your team does not have. You are in rooms they are not in. Decisions get made at the leadership level that feel small or obvious to you and land as earthquakes on the people executing underneath you.
Change is inevitable. Whiplash is not. Whiplash is what happens when change occurs without communication.

The gap between what leadership knows and what everyone else knows is where most work whiplash gets manufactured. And the only thing that closes that gap is treating who needs to know about this as a non-optional follow-up question every time a decision gets made or a priority shifts.

Work whiplash is, at its core, wasted time. When you hire someone, you are fundamentally paying for their time and their skills. Nothing should concern companies more than wasted time, and yet so much of it is wasted by bad process, bad leadership, and bad structure.

Clear delegation — one person who owns something, a handful of people who need to weigh in, an agreed-upon timeline — sounds incredibly boring. It is boring. It also prevents an enormous amount of wasted time and burned-out talent.

t: Why You Must Display Your Classroom Management Plan
q: When I visit classrooms, I rarely see a classroom management plan posted. It’s the first thing I look for.
Because it tells me a lot about the teacher. Namely, the importance they place on protecting students from disruptions in learning.
Rules and consequences posted high on the wall of your classroom send the message to everyone who enters—students, parents, and administrators alike—that learning is sacred.
A poster of your plan is a reminder to students that misbehavior is a choice they make, while enforcement is the fulfillment of a promise you made.
With your plan out in the open for all to see, you’re put on notice. You can’t escape it. It whispers to you throughout every day that you’re obligated to follow it.
I recommend writing or printing out your rules and consequences on easel-size paper or poster board and affixing it high on the front wall of your classroom.

A posted classroom management plan functions as a public symbol of trust, fairness, and objectivity that students can point back to.
Posting the plan puts the teacher on notice too, since it commits them publicly to following through on what they've displayed.
The plan should be printed on easel-size paper or poster board and mounted high on the front wall, not tucked away.

t: What If Kids' Behavior Is the Symptom, Not the Problem
q: I think school systems have gotten really efficient at scrubbing the marble.
A lot of children are just less practiced at the basic work of being human. That changes the whole conversation.
There is a category mistake hiding in plain sight. Many of the capacities schools keep trying to teach cannot be taught. They have to be grown.

Children do not develop self-regulation in the abstract. They develop it in the middle of life, when they are disappointed, excited, tired, left out, corrected, challenged, overstimulated, told no, bored, embarrassed, and then slowly learn that none of those has to become the end of the world.

A good stretch of unstructured play is doing far more than adults can see from a distance. Children are reading faces, tracking rules, testing strength, managing impulses, inventing worlds, negotiating power, recovering from embarrassment, handling exclusion, taking small risks, learning to communicate, and deciding whether the fun is worth the discomfort. It is physical, social, emotional, imaginative, moral, and cognitive all at once.

We want the finished capacities without restoring the experiences that build them. We want calm bodies with fewer chances to move. We want collaborative children with less chances to collaborate in low-stakes settings.
A well-managed child is not the same thing as a developed child. That distinction may be one of the most important lines school systems need to recover.

If the same problems keep appearing across classrooms, grade levels, families, and communities, the problem is probably bigger than the individual motivation that we keep focusing on. We have to look at the broader conditions around the child.

t: Weekly Top Five: Father's Day Edition
q: We've been telling ourselves the wrong story about fathers. For decades, American culture has largely treated fatherhood as optional, something a man can do well if he's inclined to, something admirable to witness but not essential to how kids develop and who they become.

A child cannot form a conscience from intermittent warmth. The father who appears with enthusiasm and then disappears for weeks has not failed to show up. He has shown the child that reliability is optional.

Emotional availability is not a frequency you can negotiate. It is not something you manage with good intentions and occasional grand gestures. A child's moral formation depends on the cumulative weight of a father's presence across ordinary moments.

Masculine imbalance, dominance without vulnerability and assertion without listening, corrodes the relational foundation that allows formation to occur. A child learning conscience from a father must see in that father the integration of strength and tenderness, conviction and humility.

When the state trains caseworkers not to see fathers, not to document them, not to extend to them the basic regard of recording their existence, it has not simply failed individual men. It has demonstrated to children that fathers are not worth seeing.

Presence itself has been institutionally withheld. A child's conscience forms partly through what the world tells him or her about who matters. When the world says fathers do not matter enough to track, even children whose fathers are fighting to stay present absorb a lesson about disposability.

The emotional freedom to be a good father and the structural capacity to live it out are not the same thing. A man's conscience must be coherent, integrated enough that he is not at war with himself, and his circumstances must permit him to show up consistently.

He is a man whose presence across time tells the truth every child must hear: you are seen. You matter deeply. You will be known: not once, not when it is convenient, but consistently, across the ordinariness of Tuesday evenings and small disappointments.

t: Tokenized Kids: How We Charge Students to Think
q: The single activity that produces the most actual thinking of anything we offer a teenager is the one thing we often make them pay for out of pocket.

You fund your priorities. You don't fundraise for them. The budget is the value statement, and right now the budget often says: content is the mission, and thinking is a hobby you can pursue if your parents can swing it.

We're getting ready to write enormous checks to AI companies for Socratic tutors -- software that will, supposedly, debate our kids, challenge their reasoning, ask the hard questions, build critical thinking at scale. Districts will find that money. Meanwhile, the human Socratic tutor is already in the building. She runs the debate team. She does the exact thing the software is promising -- for a stipend, after hours, while writing recommendation letters at 11pm.
The kid with the budget gets the camps, the coach, the circuit, the subscriptions -- the extended reasoning. The kid without it gets the worksheet and the free tier.

The nightmare everyone describes -- a cognitive elite that can afford the most powerful reasoning while everyone else gets throttled on the free tier -- isn't some future the machines are dragging us toward. It's a market we already built, by hand, and pointed at children.

We took the single most valuable thing we offer and made it the most exclusive. We put a paywall on critical thinking and judgment. The retrieval education stays universal -- every kid gets the worksheet -- while the thinking education quietly goes to the kids who could already afford it.
Kids shouldn't be selling donuts in the morning so they can think in the afternoon. The content is on the house. The thinking is extra.

t: The Quiet Leadership Crisis AI Is About to Expose
q: For decades, the busywork of management has provided a kind of camouflage. If you were constantly in meetings, constantly writing decks, constantly responding to emails and Slack, you looked like a leader. Your volume of activity covered the depth of impact.

Nobody had the tools, or frankly, the desire, to decouple doing a lot of management tasks from actually leading people well. The two got bundled together, and most organizations never bothered to unbundle them.

The crisis I'm talking about isn't that AI is going to take away leadership roles. The real crisis is that a large number of people currently occupying leadership roles have been getting credit for management output, not leadership impact, and that distinction is getting exposed to everyone.

Some leaders will discover, in a fairly public way, that they don't have much left once their task list is automated and managed by AI tools. Some teams are going to realize that the person who looked like their leader for years was mostly just... busy.

Some leaders, the ones who were doing the real work all along, the trust-building, the coaching, the hard conversations, the steady presence in difficult moments, are finally going to get seen for what they were actually contributing. Maybe even for the first time.

You need to get honest about your leadership impact while there's still time to close the gap, before AI closes it for you. And when it does, which will be sooner than you think, it will be very publicly, in front of your whole team.

For years, busyness was a reasonable proxy for leadership impact, because we had no better way to measure it. With AI, that proxy is disappearing, and what's left is the only thing that ever actually mattered: whether you made the people around you better.

t: The Enrollment Roller Coaster
q: Every fall, schools count their students for funding purposes. But by the time spring arrives, many of those students are gone. In most states, we don't really have a way to know how enrollment changes across the school year.

The pattern is remarkably consistent. Enrollment rises from September to October and then gradually declines throughout the rest of the school year. By May, districts are serving about 1% fewer students than they reported in October.

The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted overall enrollment levels, but it did not fundamentally change the within-year pattern. Before the pandemic and after it, Washington schools typically lost about 1% of their students between fall and spring.

States that rely on a single fall count date may be funding schools based on enrollment levels that are higher than what districts serve for much of the school year. And the patterns may be smaller than they are in places with only a single fall count.

If policymakers are basing funding and staffing models on October enrollment counts, it's a bit like designing a gym around the surge of new members who show up in January rather than the number who are still attending by spring.

t: Researchers Respond to Productive Struggle
q: We believe several critiques in Korbey's article conflate productive struggle with unproductive struggle. This distinction matters because productive struggle is not a pedagogical fad but a well-established principle of learning. Abandoning it risks returning to instructional approaches that limit students' opportunities to engage in the demanding intellectual work through which deep and lasting understanding develops.
Productive struggle is not synonymous with frustration, confusion, or repeated failure; rather, it is the effortful process through which deeper understanding develops.

Learning almost anything of value requires effort. A child learning to read struggles to connect sounds with symbols. A musician struggles to master a new piece. A teacher struggles to improve a lesson that fell short. Such effort is not harmful simply because it is difficult.

Asking students to tackle multi-digit subtraction before they have mastered prerequisite knowledge is a problem of task design, not of productive struggle. Similarly, when students lack fluency with basic facts, the appropriate response may be additional practice rather than the abandonment of challenging work.

The key to making struggle productive is teacher planning and scaffolding assistance. Hiebert and Grouws did not envision students working in isolation while teachers stand aside. Making struggle productive requires careful task selection, monitoring student thinking, providing hints and representations, asking questions, and helping students connect emerging ideas.
The teacher's role is active, not passive. A student's frustration is a call for teacher action.

The issue, then, is not whether students should struggle, but how that struggle is structured and supported. Mathematics instruction requires balance. Students need explicit instruction and deliberate practice. They also need opportunities to struggle productively, to grapple with important ideas, make conjectures, test strategies, and learn from mistakes.

t: Lessons Worth Arguing About
q: Take negative numbers. Someone shares their preferred introduction -- debt and borrowing, or a thermometer dipping below zero, or the abstract number line, or a physical line that pupils walk along -- and the replies fill with teachers who have thought about this for years and settled on something different.

The closer you look at a canonical lesson, the harder it becomes to say what teaching it well actually requires. Why doesn’t learning science give us clear principles for exactly the lessons where the stakes are highest?

A teacher who insists on the most generalisable model is teaching for a payoff that arrives later, and pays for it now. And they do so with no immediate signal to tell them that the payoff is worthwhile.

The hard instructional questions do not usually arise because one side has a principle and the other side has a prejudice. They arise because both sides have a principle that is worthy of application.

When a teacher deliberates between the diving board and the debt model, they are not inventing new pedagogy. They are adjudicating between principles they already hold: deciding how much comprehensibility is worth giving up for generalisability, for this concept, with these learners, at this point in the sequence.
When experienced teachers argue about a first representation, they are not failing to apply the science; they are doing the part of the work the science has not yet reached -- arguing about weights.

t: Curios of the Week #172
q: In Victoria, there exists a bureaucratic ratio of one bureaucrat for every two teachers, while in Queensland, this ratio stands at one bureaucrat for just under two teachers. These ratios are purportedly justified by the implementation of various educational models, school reviews, wellbeing programs, and teaching and learning incentives. However, none of these initiatives have demonstrated positive outcomes.

TPAA is part of the Red Union movement and grew to prominence during COVID by opposing vaccine mandates. In 2024, a group of education academics wrote a paper condemning TPAA as an astroturf organisation. However, if you read their paper, you will see they provide little evidence for this.

Significantly, the authors also disclose they are supporters of traditional unions, one of which funded their research into TPAA -- research that mainly involved looking at TPAA's social media accounts.

The paper rightly identifies critical pedagogy as a malign influence that the current system does not weed out due to a lack of reality checks and accountability. If it were only critical pedagogy we had to deal with, then that would be an improvement on the current situation in which we are bombarded by bad ideas from everywhere.

In his covering letter, Scott Stanford, the national president, notes that traditional unions donate to the Australian Labor Party. He does not object to this but he suggests there should be industrial representation available for people who don't want to subsidise a political party. Which is a fair point.

t: Admiration May Be the Most Underrated Leadership Tool
q: Of the 27 emotions identified by psychologists, admiration is perhaps the most underrated and underleveraged by leaders. That's because leaders are taught to seek admiration, not to find and give it.

Admiration signals what a leader values and reveals what they believe matters most. Being genuinely admired by someone you respect is one of the most powerful motivators in human experience. It doesn't just feel good. It shapes self-identity.

Admiration felt and expressed by leaders sets the thermostat for how people operate. When a leader admires boldness, people take more risks. When they admire precision, people slow down and get it right.
People strive to become the version of themselves that their leaders admire. In that sense, admiration creates a mirror, and people grow into the reflection.

Unlike praise or flattery, which are things leaders say, admiration is an emotion leaders feel through observation and reflection. It is always highly specific and arises from what leaders find exceptional and impressive in others.

The best leaders are more likely to admire the effort behind what a person does, the way they do it, and what it says about their character rather than just their outcomes or results. They are acutely aware of what they admire and why.

Admiration costs nothing, does not require formal authority, and carries no agenda. It is simply honest, specific recognition of what a leader genuinely finds exceptional in another person. Yet its impact is transformative.

t: Why the Best People Leave First
q: The order of exits is a signal. Most leaders assume it's turnover. It's not.
Your best people have options. They always do. When they leave, it's not because they couldn't find work somewhere else. It's because they couldn't find what they needed here.
The A-players leave. Then the B-players start looking. Then you're left building with what remains, wondering what happened to the team you thought you had.
If you're the one being left, don't waste the signal. The best people are telling you something on their way out. The only question is whether you're able to hear it.
Fixing the system that drove them out matters more than replacing the person who left. Replace without fixing, and you'll lose the replacement too.
x: Kelly McGinnis argues that when turnover happens, the departure order is not random -- the best performers leave first, and this pattern is a diagnostic signal that most leaders misread as ordinary attrition.

t: The Quiet Reinvention of Assessment
q: Two years ago we acknowledged AI had broken assessment. Initially, the reaction was defensive. In higher education, AI bans, huge investment in AI detection tools and a return to in-person examination were standard in 2024.
Meanwhile, in corporate L&D;, many of us worried that employees were quietly outsourcing their learning to AI—going through the motions of assessment without actually developing the capability.
The real problem with most assessments was not that AI could do them—it was that they were never really measuring what we said they were measuring in the first place.
Performance-based assessment requires the learner to be present. You cannot delegate presence. You cannot outsource judgment. You cannot submit a live demonstration.
What AI has done is reveal the gap between assessment-as-compliance and assessment-as-evidence-of-capability. The gap was always there. Now it is impossible to ignore.

t: The Discipline of Using Transitions to Revisit Expectations
q: Over time, the performance expectations shared by leaders and team members tend to become cloudy and less complete.

Differences in perceptions and expectations accumulate quietly, one small assumption at a time. Eventually, the gap between what a leader expects and what a team member delivers grows wide enough to cause real concern or even damage.

When the calendar turns to a new year, when a team member earns a promotion, when a project schedule changes, or when someone steps into a new role or assignment, something shifts in the psychological landscape.
Ask yourself a simple question: What transition is coming up that could serve as a gateway to resetting expectations? Use the segue to do just that.
Close the gap between expectations and performance. This discipline benefits everyone.

t: The Best Manager in the Company Has to Be You
q: The quality of a company at scale is equal to the quality of the management team.
Every mediocre manager is a hidden tax. You pay it in missed goals, in talent you didn't keep, in decisions that got made badly or not at all.
The product can carry you for a while. The mission can carry you. But eventually the management team becomes the binding constraint on everything you're trying to build.
If you want a world-class company, you have to insist on world-class management. That starts with you. Not as a standard you impose on others, but as a commitment you make to yourself.
Developing great managers is not a luxury or an HR function. It is the strategic work of leadership.

t: A Vision for Teaching English
q: English is the study of language both as a means of living and as a tool for human thought. A high-quality English curriculum allows pupils to participate fully in the world and fosters their sense of belonging within it.

Through confident reading and attentive listening, pupils not only allow others to communicate successfully with them, they enter the wider conversation in which literature records and reshapes human experience. The study of English becomes a gateway to deep wells of thought and experience beyond their own.

The intensely personal pleasure of immersion in the flow of well-crafted prose makes a text a place to live inside and where a pupil makes meaning at their own pace. Whether through the narrative tension and fully imagined world of a novel or through an intricately crafted argument, a literary text captivates the readers mind.

Vocabulary runs through every aspect of the subject. Words function as conceptual tools that enable pupils to make finer distinctions, perceive pattern and hold more complex ideas in mind. As vocabulary expands, so does the reach of thought.

A cumulative approach shapes the teaching of reading, writing and spoken language. Reading fluency and disciplinary knowledge must be built step by step. In Foundation and Key Stage 1, this means that phonological awareness and decoding ability are priorities until automaticity, accuracy and prosody are achieved by all.

Wide reading reveals how writers connect across time, genre and tradition. Through knowledge of context and intertextuality, pupils learn that stories do not stand alone but belong to a shared cultural landscape in which ideas are inherited, contested and refined.

q: An elementary teacher I'll call Ms. Smith emailed me because she was distraught at a test-prep lesson she had just observed: Students were given a six-paragraph excerpt from The Diary of Anne Frank and asked to 'infer' how Anne felt about her friends — which, Anne confided to her diary in the excerpt, she no longer had. The kids knew nothing of Anne Frank, including the fact that she was hiding in an attic, or of World War II.

t: The Slide Designer Trap
q: I want to take you back in time to 2015, the year I started my initial teacher training. I was placed in a fantastic school with brilliant colleagues, a supportive atmosphere, and an abundance of good intentions. Yet, it was during this exact year that my relationship with planning became toxic, setting off a cycle where I risked burning out more times than I care to admit.

All of a sudden, my days were entirely hijacked by digital design. This endless scramble to build PowerPoint decks took a massive toll. It stripped away the physical and mental time I desperately needed to develop and practise the other core competencies required of an educator.

I wasn't handed a single base slide to start from. Instead, I was pointed toward a chaotic shared drive, a digital graveyard of unorganised folders, random PDF files, and fragmented decks from years gone by. To survive the next morning, I found myself working until 2:00 AM, scouring the internet for worksheets, clipping images, and aligning text boxes.

The only reason I didn't join the statistics of those who quit during their training year was an intense, stubborn love for teaching and a deep pool of intrinsic motivation. I gritted my teeth, passed my training, and officially entered the profession.

I fell into the trap of believing that if my slides looked flawless and I followed them line by line, the lesson would be a success. It was a lie. Static, hyper-designed slides don't make a lesson successful; in fact, they actively sabotage your ability to deliver true responsive teaching.

Students do not care about your slide transitions, custom fonts, or colour palettes. They don't need a graphic designer. They are perfectly happy with a piece of paper, a visualiser, or a blank whiteboard, provided they are being taught by a teacher who has the energy, clarity, and focus to teach them properly.

Schools are accidentally sending a message to both new and veteran teachers that their primary value lies in their ability to curate digital assets, rather than their ability to deliver explicit instruction, scaffold learning, and manage a classroom.

The introduction of fully planned, high-quality, centralised lesson resources is not a luxury; it is an absolute necessity. When a school provides an established, evidence-based instructional framework as a baseline, teachers are instantly liberated.” Archived from Dr Dario Emanuele (Substack) on June 19, 2026 by Tim.

t: Shaped by Default: From Narrative Capture to Deliberate Shaping
q: This is the equivalent of making a wish in front of a birthday cake, changing nothing about how you live, and assuming the wish will find its way to you. Most strategy development takes this shape: declare a vision, let the machine run, produce the Greek Temple, amplify the narrative to the world, and try to optimise the parts while the whole fails to produce the effect required to shape the external environment to your advantage.

An organisation shaped by its own narrative has also lost the ability to see who is configuring the conditions it takes for granted. Leaders withdraw from or lose influence in the forums where direction is set, learning of decisions after they have happened.

The control reflex and better narratives only address symptoms. The only thing that addresses the root cause is rebuilding the capacity to see clearly, which means investing in organisational intelligence.

Framing is owning the narrative space; it is shaping how other actors understand the situation before acting on it. The organisation that shapes what the relevant actors treat as the obvious problem and the sensible response has done something more durable than any structural intervention.

Binding shapes others by constraining the organisation's own options, because doing so changes what the other parties decide. It rests on the paradox that the power to constrain another may depend on the power to bind oneself, and that the deliberate, irreversible surrender of a freedom can be a source of strength.

The external environment is not passive; it does not wait for you to be ready. Other actors are working on the conditions that will determine what is possible next. The organisation that has only been shaped will meet reality on terms it did not set and cannot easily change.

t: I'm Terrified: Struggling to Take My Own Advice on This Graduation Day
q: Graduation is a chance to give one last smile. One last, 'Good luck!' One last, 'Thank you!' One last demonstration that we're glad and grateful we had the chance to be their teacher. One last time to show them we're happy they were a part of our lives for a few brief years. Seems like an evening well spent to me.
There's even a selfish part of me that would prefer my students' last impression of 'Mr. G' to be a memory of the me who had a strong voice.

Strangely, those fears are both paralyzing and irrelevant. I don't believe in fate, but it does feel like my actions are already decided. If my choices are (a) risk revealing how injured my voice actually is, or (b) risk my students thinking I forgot about them, then there is no choice.

I honestly don't know how I will feel as I drive home from my former school's graduation. It's very possible that, in that moment, I will feel worse for attending the ceremony. However, I am absolutely certain that the next day, a year from now, and for the rest of the time I have on this earth, I will feel better for having gone.

Seeing my students celebrate their accomplishments gave me some of the best memories from my career. That's why I always advised my student teachers to go to their school's graduation, even if — especially if — they're not required to.

t: Fighting the Anchoring Bias in Negotiations
q: In what is known as 'anchoring bias,' the first offer or proposal in a negotiation becomes a psychological mooring that sets the baseline.
Even though people can counter with whatever they choose, most people allow this anchor to define the parameters of the exchange.
Even if the team member were convinced that $160,000 reflects the true market value, they normally won't ask for that salary because of the anchor.
The anchoring bias exists in nearly all negotiations, so it is critical to remember that whoever offers the first proposal implicitly sets the tone for the negotiation.
Good negotiators don't let the opening proposal dictate their approach. They insist on exploring all the options available as if the opening offer were written in pencil, not ink.
x: The first offer in a negotiation becomes a psychological anchor that constrains all subsequent counteroffers, regardless of its basis in actual value.
Anchoring bias operates even when negotiators are aware of it: knowing about the anchor does not neutralize it -- only deliberate reanchoring strategies can counter it.
Leaders should train teams to identify anchoring in real time: whether negotiating salary, contracts, or budgets, recognizing the anchor in the moment is the prerequisite for countering it.
Admired Leadership examines anchoring bias, the cognitive phenomenon in which the first offer in any negotiation disproportionately shapes all subsequent counteroffers.
Skilled negotiators don't accept the frame of the opening offer: they treat it as written in pencil and insist on exploring the full range of options before moving toward a number.

t: Your Mind Gets the Gist in 100 Milliseconds
q: You quickly get the 'gist' of what's happening. You automatically sense what's there before you think about it or what words describe it. The same is true when you view a work of art, notice someone's emotions, or hear a sound.
Gist processing feels obvious, but has real scientific weight. For example, we know it takes about 100 milliseconds for us to get the gist of a scene. That's a blink of the eye.
She wanted to know: when does meaning start to form? Her work showed that it happens faster than anyone thought possible.
Imagine a skilled chess player glancing at a board—they don't see individual pieces but patterns, positions, and possibilities. They've chunked their knowledge into compressed, meaningful units.
The gist we get from a scene is the seed of understanding. It's how new information starts to stick, and it sets the stage for everything that follows.
x: Lee LeFever explores the neuroscience of "gist processing"—the brain's near-instantaneous capacity to extract the essence of a scene before conscious attention engages.

Drawing on MIT cognitive psychologist Mary Potter's landmark research, LeFever explains that the mind grasps the meaning of an image or scene in roughly 100 milliseconds, far faster than anyone had assumed.

t: Writing Instruction: A Cat With Nine Lives Hanging On By Its Tail in Texas
q: What I saw for years was that because it was only tested in fourth and seventh grade, students would only get explicit writing instruction in fourth and seventh grade.

As a seventh-grade teacher, I would be scrambling to try to figure out how can I cover all of these grammar mechanics? How do I cover all of these writing techniques? What can I drop? What do we need to focus on?

Legislation early in the 2020s required TEA to reduce its reliance on multiple-choice items in favor of constructed-response items. Researchers in writing assessment have long documented the unfortunate consequences of grade-level targeting of writing.

Erika De La Rosa was right to hope. She was right to be disappointed. The obligation now is to keep saying clearly what is being lost before the generation that never learned to write inherits the consequences.
Everything we know about how human beings develop as thinkers through language is at stake in these decisions about writing instruction and assessment.

t: Why People With Half Your Talent Seem to Keep Winning
q: The uncomfortable truth about career growth: talent is not enough -- visibility, advocacy, and manager alignment turn hard work into promotion.
Two people can do identical work. One gets promoted. The other gets stuck wondering why. The difference is rarely effort. It's almost always visibility and advocacy.
Your manager cannot advocate for what they do not know. Keeping your head down and delivering excellent results is a strategy that works only if someone is watching.
The people who seem to win with half your talent have figured out that careers are built at the intersection of competence and connection.
This is not about politics. It's about understanding how decisions get made and ensuring that the people who make them have accurate information about your contributions.

t: Why History Textbooks Suck
q: Perhaps, like many people, you think the problem with textbooks is that they are 'biased' or don't tell 'the truth,' about the past. Or that they focus on only political history or stories about white men and leave out other people and groups.
Coverage doesn't equal understanding. In fact, the relentless drive to cover everything is precisely what makes it impossible to understand anything.
What students need is not more facts about more events, but the conceptual tools to make sense of the facts they do encounter—a framework for understanding why history unfolds the way it does.
History textbooks are organized for the convenience of curriculum committees, not for the cognitive needs of students. The result is a form of coverage that defeats its own purpose.
When we flatten complex events into bullet points, we don't just lose the details. We lose the very thing that makes history worth learning: the ability to reason about human action and consequence.

The textbook problem is architectural, not ideological: the coverage model—trying to fit all of history into one book—structurally prevents the deep engagement needed for understanding and retention.
Chronological organization without narrative arc produces a sequence of events that students cannot interpret: students need causal explanation and thematic coherence, not just chronological facts.

t: When Cognitive Science Becomes a Checklist: The Problem with Generic Lesson Structures
q: When cognitive science is translated into a fixed lesson structure, something important is lost. Research findings become visible rituals. Principles become phases. Professional judgement becomes compliance.

Kirschner, Sweller and Clark argue that novices usually need strong instructional guidance because unguided discovery can overload working memory. That is a powerful principle. It is not a command to place teacher explanation and modelling at point two in every lesson.

For an ECT, a structure may offer useful security at first, but if it becomes the measure of good teaching, it can prevent them from learning how to make principled decisions. They may learn to ask, Have I included retrieval and modelling? rather than, What does this class need to understand this concept?
For an experienced, effective teacher, the structure can become a ceiling rather than a floor. Over time, this shifts expertise from responsive decision-making to visible compliance.

A better lesson planning model would not begin with phases. It would begin with learning and learning problems. What should pupils know or be able to do by the end? Why is this difficult? What do they already know?

t: Foundational Skills for Older Readers: What the Research Actually Says
q: Sarah opened with a reminder that can get lost when the conversation turns to decoding and fluency: comprehension is the goal. Always. Everything else—morphology, word reading, fluency instruction—exists in service of that.

She offered a metaphor that landed for the group. Think of comprehension like a field of daisies. Some students walk through and pick one. Some pick a few. Some pick a handful. All three understood the passage—just at different depths.
We cannot assume that older students who struggle with fluency will simply grow out of it through exposure. They need explicit, targeted instruction delivered with intention.
What we know about morphology is that it's one of the highest-leverage things we can teach at the secondary level. One root can unlock dozens of academic words across multiple content areas.
The goal is always to bring students back to meaning. Foundational skills instruction that never connects to comprehension is practicing a fire drill that never serves in a real fire.

t: Everyone Is Transforming. Nobody Is Integrating.
q: In her experience, the word integration usually meant that several things had already failed to meet one another in the wild, and a group of tired people had now been assembled to admire the gap. Still, the meeting was necessary. That was the trouble. Almost everything in it was necessary.
In practice, this meant she spent a lot of her time working out which version of reality needed to be made believable to whom, by when, and at what cost to the people below the official account.

Maya wrote that phrase down, partly because it sounded important and partly because she wanted to remember it for later, when someone would inevitably be manually reconciling three spreadsheets because the frictionless intelligence had encountered a local data definition.

Absorption says: I will work harder so this still looks manageable. Integration says: let us look at what is being made manageable, by whom, and at what cost. Absorption says: I will translate the contradiction so others can keep moving. Integration says: the contradiction is data; we need to bring it into the room without letting it destroy the room.

The earlier question is: what has this system failed to integrate before asking Maya to lead? Once that is asked, the leadership work changes. Maya still has to influence the room. t: Do You Nag People?
q: Nagging is a persuasion cycle where one person repeatedly makes the same request and the other person resists or withdraws, frustrating both parties. In relationships, this pattern is linked to defensiveness, dissatisfaction, and weak compliance. In other words, nagging doesn't usually work unless the goal is to annoy or irritate the other party.

Nagging erodes trust and mutual influence, creating a pattern where one partner feels unheard and the other feels pressured. This produces relational stress, emotional distance, and topic avoidance, making the relationship less durable over time.

Nagging often becomes self-reinforcing: one person nags more because they feel ignored, and the other withdraws more because they feel overwhelmed. This escalation can turn a solvable issue into a chronic communication pattern that is highly poisonous once it takes hold.

In the workplace, leaders sometimes fall into the pattern of nagging without realizing it. They often believe escalating reminders are necessary to get tasks and projects completed on time. This is especially true when they think they are 'driving accountability.'

Leaders who repeatedly press for answers, updates, and commitments are naggers. Because they often interpret their own nagging behavior as producing urgency, clarity, and quality, they view repeated pressure as healthy persistence and fail to see the withdrawal and resistance it creates.

Good leaders refrain from nagging. Instead, they clarify expectations, ensure people understand the purpose behind the assignment, and check in respectfully to learn about roadblocks or delays. When they must be persistent, they address any gap in progress directly and discuss what is reducing performance without falling into the negative pattern of demand-withdraw.” Archived from Admired Leadership (Substack) on June 19, 2026 by Tim.

t: Two things can be true at once: teacher education in Australia, evidence and the human work of teaching
q: Two things can be true at once. Teacher attrition is a systemic problem, rooted in workload, pay, status, accountability, conditions and the erosion of professional trust. And teacher education still needs to take seriously what we know about how pupils learn.

Skourdoumbis and Rowe similarly critique the mandating of brain science in initial teacher education, warning that a narrow what works approach can become reductionist, standardised and deprofessionalising.

A technocratic approach says: The evidence says this works, so implement it. A professional approach says: This evidence helps us understand a problem of learning. Now, given this subject, this class, this curriculum, these pupils and this moment, what is the best professional decision?
This is the difference between evidence as a cage and evidence as a compass. Evidence becomes a cage when it is used to close down argument, flatten context or remove teacher agency.
Two things can be true at once. The system needs reform. And teacher education needs to teach how students learn. The challenge is to do both without reducing either the teacher or the child.

t: AI Tools Have the Potential to Widen the Performance Gap Between High and Low Performers
q: When team members use AI to augment their work, both high and low performers benefit from the ideas, strategies, and suggestions the tools produce.
In contexts where problems are broad, complex, or fuzzy, AI doesn't replace human judgment — it amplifies it.

These low performers act on the AI guidance without thinking critically about it. To their detriment.
AI deployments actually risk widening performance gaps, because the people who need it the most are usually the least equipped to filter and apply the advice it offers.

t: There's No Better Feeling Than Knowing You're Getting Better
q: Clark believes that one thing motivates high performers more than anything else— a leader who invests in making people better.
In Clark’s view, there is no better feeling in the world than knowing you are making progress and getting better.
Every time he points out that a player has made marked improvement, he earns their implicit permission to demand even more.
It is this balance of magnified strengths and intense feedback that propels them forward, allowing continuous progress and improvement.
The most effective path to high performance runs through growth, not just achievement.

t: We Bulldozed the Ecosystem of Childhood Then Blamed Kids For Struggling
q: We have cleared away so much of the natural habitat children used to grow inside. Not cruelly. Not usually on purpose. Most of the time, we had reasons that made sense in the moment. Safety. Convenience. Busy schedules. Academic pressure. Liability. But little by little, we cleared the natural habitat of childhood.
Then children show up in school hungry for the exact capacities a healthy childhood habitat used to give them, and we blame the kids for not having them.

A child used to practice frustration tolerance by losing a backyard game and having to keep playing because going inside meant there was nothing to do except stare at wallpaper and reconsider your life choices.

We took away the reps the childhood ecosystem provided. Then we got surprised when children looked underdeveloped. We started lifting the weight for the child each time a struggle came up then wondered why they were so weak in self-regulation, executive function, interpersonal skills, and self-direction.
A support is not the same thing as an ecosystem. A deer eating my school garden may need a better fence. But the fence does not explain why the deer are suddenly there more often.

Because children are not supposed to grow up inside a world where every hour is scheduled, every conflict is mediated, every risk is softened, every silence is filled, every boredom is treated as a problem, every movement is contained, and every social experience is either adult-run or screen-based.
And when children do not get enough room to become capable, their needs do not disappear. They just show up somewhere. Usually in the least convenient place possible.
