t: To Script or Not to Script
q: The critique I hear most often is: 'Scripts turn teachers into robots.' I understand the concern. A teacher who is word-for-word reading to students from a binder doesn't look like a professional. But that critique misidentifies what the scripted part of teaching actually is.

When I teach a scripted lesson, I'm not a robot. I'm a professional with both hands free. The language of instruction has been worked out in advance -- by researchers, by curriculum designers, by people who have taught this content to thousands of children. I don't need to use my cognitive bandwidth on what to say. I need it all for what I'm seeing.

The novice teacher is managing everything simultaneously: the content, the language, the pacing, the behavior, the individual child who doesn't understand, the child who is ahead. A script removes one of those burdens. It is not a constraint. It is a gift.

Reading Mastery is not a script because someone wanted to control teachers. It is a script because the people who designed it spent decades figuring out the clearest, most effective way to introduce phonemic awareness to a struggling reader, and they wrote it down so you don't have to reinvent it.

The question isn't 'should teachers have professional judgment?' Of course they should. The question is what professional judgment is for. It's for reading the room, responding to the child, deciding when to go back and when to push forward. A good script is not the enemy of that work. It is what makes that work possible.

t: Stop Letting the Professor Be the First Person to Find the Flaws
q: Here is the design problem with traditional writing feedback: the professor is the first person to read the paper critically. Every logical gap, every unsupported claim, every structural weakness -- the professor finds it first. Students have been submitting work that has never been stress-tested by anyone except the person who will grade it.

The Red Team Advisor doesn't help you write. It attacks what you've written. It looks for the weakest point in your argument and pushes on it. It finds the assumption you forgot to justify. It identifies the evidence that doesn't quite support the claim you're hanging on it.

The Rubric Board is five evaluators, each assigned to one dimension of the grading rubric. You submit your draft and each evaluator gives you feedback from their specific angle. You see what a thesis grader would see, what a mechanics grader would see, what an evidence grader would see -- before your professor sees any of it.

These aren't one-time prompts. You save them as Claude project instructions. Every paper your student writes this semester, they bring to the same two advisors. The advisors become familiar. The student starts to anticipate what the Red Team will find. That anticipation is the metacognitive development we're trying to produce.

The goal is not for AI to fix the paper. The goal is for the student to fix the paper after the AI has told them what's broken. The authorial work stays with the student. What changes is how much information they have before they decide the paper is done.

t: Research Bite #68: Worked Examples and Self-Explanation Prompts
q: This study followed up on a US randomised controlled trial of MathByExample — supplemental maths worksheets that alternate correct and incorrect worked examples with self-explanation prompts. The original trial showed the materials raised standardised test scores; here the researchers asked whether they also shifted students’ motivation.

Using data from 1,230 fourth and fifth graders, they examined four beliefs: maths self-concept, interest, perceived importance, and a less-studied one — perceived functionality of errors (how useful students think mistakes are).

Two findings stand out. First, the error belief positively predicted maths achievement, even after accounting for the others. Second, despite their proven learning benefits, the materials produced no significant change in any of the four motivation measures across the school year.

1,230 US elementary students — 709 in Grade 5, 521 in Grade 4 — across 58 classes in 17 schools and five districts, taught by 37 teachers. The sample was 57.4% male, 32.9% female; 52% were from underrepresented minority groups.

Don’t assume error-friendly materials will change error-friendly beliefs. This is the study’s sharpest lesson. The same worksheets had previously raised test scores, yet a full year of working with incorrect examples shifted none of the four motivation beliefs — including the one about errors.

In a surprising result, students who rated maths as more important actually scored slightly lower. The authors suspect pressure may be at work. It's a tentative finding, but a useful nudge: emphasising the interest and usefulness of maths may serve students better than stressing how vital it is that they're good at it.

Our findings highlight that despite significant learning gains, perceived functionality of errors, self-concept, interest, and perceptions of importance remained stable, indicating that students’ beliefs about their math abilities may be more resistant to change than their actual performance.

t: Limbic Capitalism Has Been Driving Addiction for Hundreds of Years
q: The story of psychoactive substances and addictive behaviors is, in large measure, the story of the limbic system being targeted, exploited, and in some cases rewired by industries that understood, intuitively and then scientifically, how to trigger its reward pathways.

Merchants didn't need neuroscience to discover that certain products sold better when they were more concentrated, more accessible, and accompanied by social rituals that normalized use. They discovered this through the oldest form of research: watching what people would pay for and keep coming back for.

The limbic system doesn't distinguish between ancient pleasures and modern ones. Tobacco, slot machines, and Instagram feeds light up the same reward circuits. The brain that evolved to prize sugar, sex, and status is the same brain that checks its phone 150 times a day.

Every era of limbic capitalism has required structural intervention to contain. Prohibition failed, but taxation, age restrictions, advertising bans, and plain packaging all worked at the margins. Individual willpower has never been sufficient, and there is no reason to expect it to suffice now.

The smartphone and social media industries are not uniquely evil. They are doing what limbic industries have always done: finding the most effective stimulus, reducing friction to the vanishing point, and scaling. What is new is the speed, the targeting precision, and the age at which the hook is set.

q: **_Disclosure:_**_ While I have no business relationship with the California Community College system, I was involved in helping them set up the Online Education Initiative, which was renamed the California Virtual Campus. So the real question is not "what's wrong with online education." It is how a course like this gets offered at all, inside a system that has spent more than a decade building an apparatus designed to avoid these problems. Since 2014, CCCS, through the Online Education Initiative that was renamed as the California Virtual Campus (CVC), have run a voluntary course-design rubric and a Peer Online Course Review process (POCR) that not only provides guidance on design but also puts faculty courses...

The failure CalMatters found is real -- but it is a failure of local commitment, a campus where the quality process is optional, and a department let an indefensible course run. It is not a failure of online education.

That study was based on the primary metric shared in CCC public data - course completion rates with grades of A, B, or C. This, of course, is not an ideal metric, which can be seen in the aforementioned microeconomics course example. Passing that course would be easy, whether you learned anything or not.

Furthermore, the pandemic presented an outlier, where most students were forced into online courses in "emergency remote learning" situations. **If you look at the pre- and post-pandemic years, what jumps out to me is the significant increase in performance for online course taking with much smaller increases for traditional, or face-to-face course taking. In fact, the performance gap has all but disappeared in the system.**

If the CalMatters' headline of "Community college students struggle with online education" refers to students having to work hard, then that would make sense. But what I believe they actually mean is that students are not succeeding because of online education.

q: Think about electricity. We didn't ask whether electricity was good or bad for manufacturing. We asked how to rebuild manufacturing around electric power. Higher education is organized around information scarcity. The professor knows things the student does not. The library has books you cannot find elsewhere. The credential signals that you sat in rooms with people who knew things. All of that made sense in 1960. Almost none of it makes sense in 2026.

Accreditation is the hidden hand that shapes everything downstream. As long as accreditation frameworks reward seat time rather than demonstrated competency, institutions cannot redesign around learning outcomes without risking their funding.

AI literacy is not an elective. It is a general education requirement. In 1960, we decided that every college graduate needed to be able to write an essay and reason quantitatively. t: Bob Wasn't Loyal, He Was Trapped
q: At Bob's retirement party, his manager called him 'one of the most loyal employees IBM has ever had.' Bob smiled. His wife smiled. Everyone applauded. And I thought: loyal to what, exactly? To a company that restructured his division three times? To work he described, when I asked him privately, as 'fine, I guess'?

Bob stayed for 38 years because leaving at year 15 would have cost him his pension. Because his health insurance was IBM's. Because his mortgage was sized to his IBM salary. Because at year 20 he started telling himself 'might as well stay for 40.'

What organizations call loyalty is almost always structural capture. The golden handcuffs are effective. The pension cliff works. The health insurance lock-in works. What they produce is compliant bodies, not engaged minds.

The loyal employee shows up differently than the trapped one. They bring an idea on Tuesday afternoon not because they have to, not because it's in their KPIs, but because they give a damn. You can feel the difference in a room.
Build something people stay in because they want to, not because they can't afford to leave. The loyalty you earn that way is the only kind worth having.

t: 5 Ways Fathers Fail at Early Childhood Discipline
q: The window for habit formation opens earlier than most fathers realize. Between 12 and 18 months, your child is laying down behavioral patterns that will persist for years. Most dads wait until three or four, when they think the kid 'understands.' By then, you're correcting habits, not forming them.

Anger is information. Your toddler reads your anger and learns: this is serious. But anger alone cannot teach the alternative behavior. It marks the boundary without building the road. That's why fathers who rely only on anger have children who know what they shouldn't do but not what they should.

Every command you don't enforce teaches the same lesson: you don't have to listen. 'Stop that or we're leaving' -- but you don't leave. 'Don't do that again' -- but you tolerate it again. The child is not defiant. The child is a scientist, and your behavior is the data. They have correctly concluded that your commands are optional.

Discipline is a pattern, not an event. Your toddler is not going to remember the one time you sat down calmly and explained why hitting is wrong. They will remember -- at the level of conditioned response -- the 200 times you responded consistently and proportionately to the behavior.

When you say 'ask your mom' every time, you are not delegating. You are withdrawing. You are teaching your child that you are not a source of answers, limits, or safety. That lesson will persist long after they stop asking about bedtime.

t: Why English Examiners Struggle
q: The single most powerful finding in the Ofqual research is the 44% exact agreement rate. One in two times, two trained examiners looking at the same script disagreed on the mark. This is not a rounding error. It is the system working as designed -- and it should change how we teach.

Ofqual identified four main sources of examiner error: not applying the mark scheme consistently; not reading the whole response before beginning to mark; allowing performance on one question to influence marking of another; and substituting personal preferences for published criteria.

AO6 is where the disagreement is worst. Holistic judgments about writing quality are the hardest to standardise, because they require the examiner to weigh multiple features simultaneously against a descriptor that cannot fully specify what 'good' looks like in every possible student response.

If examiners systematically disagree about holistic writing quality, the intelligent response is to ensure your students' writing contains features about which there is relatively little disagreement: technical accuracy, vocabulary range, sentence variety.

The 56% disagreement rate does not mean English is subjective in a way that renders assessment meaningless. It means English contains a legitimate evaluative dimension that we have not yet found a way to standardise -- and that teachers who understand this can build it into their instruction.

Teaching students to write for the mark scheme is not a corruption of English education. The mark scheme is an attempt to operationalise what skilled writing looks like. Teaching students to satisfy it explicitly is teaching them what skilled writing actually requires -- made unusually legible.

t: The Use of Context in Assessment
q: When we talk about context in assessment, we often assume that more context means more accessible. Karl Maton's work invites us to question that assumption. A contextualised question does not remove cognitive demand -- it relocates it.

Semantic gravity is high when knowledge is tied strongly to its context of application; it is low when knowledge is abstract and context-independent. Neither end of the spectrum is inherently harder, but they demand different cognitive moves from students.

The semantic wave is the pedagogical gold standard: moving students from the abstract to the concrete and back again, repeatedly, until the journey in both directions is fluent. Assessment that stays at one extreme tests only half the wave.

When an examiner writes a question about a shopping trolley in a supermarket car park, they are not making physics more friendly. They are requiring students to perform an act of context-stripping: to look past the trolley and see the force diagram hiding behind it. That is a skill. It should be taught.

The equity problem with contextualised assessment is not that disadvantaged students are less intelligent. It is that unfamiliar contexts impose a dual cognitive load: process the context and retrieve the concept simultaneously.

Good curriculum design rides semantic waves deliberately. The concept is introduced abstractly, embodied in a context, stripped back to the abstract again, then embedded in a new context. By the third or fourth wave, students can move fluently in both directions -- and that fluency is what contextualised assessment is actually measuring.

t: The Irreplaceable Interpreter
q: I came across Charles Sanders Peirce's theory of signs and found in it not a philosophical curiosity but a precise diagnosis of what is at stake when we ask an AI to help a student understand a text.

In Peirce's system, the interpretant is not the person doing the interpreting. It is the meaning-effect produced in that person by their encounter with the sign. It is irreducibly theirs. It cannot be pre-formed by another mind and delivered intact. The moment you deliver it, it becomes your interpretant, not theirs.

When a student asks an AI to explain what a poem means and the AI explains, the student does not receive an interpretation. They receive the AI's interpretant. They now possess a meaning they did not make. This is not learning. This is, in the most precise sense, the opposite of learning.

The question is not whether AI interpretations are accurate. They often are. The question is what kind of mind is formed by a childhood of receiving accurate interpretations rather than struggling toward imperfect ones.

Peirce saw that semiosis -- the process of meaning-making -- is never finished. Every interpretant becomes a new sign, which calls forth a new interpretant, in an infinite chain of meaning-making. Education is the deliberate cultivation of this capacity.

The teacher's irreplaceability is not sentimental. It is structural. The teacher is the third term in the semiotic relation -- the one whose presence transforms the sign-object encounter into an occasion for the student's interpretant to form.

t: Physical Health and Coordination: The Architecture of Childhood
q: At some point in the last thirty years, we decided that keeping children safe from physical risk was more important than giving their developing nervous systems what they actually need. We got the safety. We are now discovering what we traded for it.

The cerebellum, long considered purely a motor structure, is now understood to be involved in cognitive timing, attention regulation, and even emotional modulation. When we deprive a child of the physical experiences that develop the cerebellum, we are not just limiting their athleticism. We are limiting their mind.

Gross motor development is not a warm-up act for the real show of academic learning. It is, in the first years of life, the primary medium through which children understand their world -- space, force, causality, the resistance of objects, the unpredictability of other people.

Every hour a young child spends on a screen is an hour not spent in the kind of whole-body, socially embedded, physically risky play that their nervous system is trying to wire itself for. That is not a moral claim. It is a neurological one.

What fine motor development gives a child is not just the ability to hold a pencil. It is the ability to control a tool -- to apply intention through an instrument with precision. That capacity, practiced thousands of times in the first years of life, is a transferable skill in the deepest sense.

The Architecture of Childhood is not metaphorical. There is a sequence to it. Physical competence comes first -- not because it matters more, but because it builds the platform on which everything else rests.

t: Learning Isn't Enough
q: I spend a lot of time thinking about why smart organisations with good intentions keep failing to change how they work, even after they've invested in learning. The answer is almost never the quality of the learning. It's almost always the culture they send people back into.

Learning is the beginning of a process, not the end of one. What you know after a workshop is raw material. What determines whether that raw material becomes changed behaviour is whether the environment you return to gives you permission to be bad at something new long enough to get good at it.

Tolerance for imperfection is not a soft cultural nice-to-have. It is the mechanical precondition for skill acquisition. You cannot get from knowing to doing without passing through a period of doing it badly. Organisations that reward performance above all else punish the transition -- and then wonder why people don't change.

Protected practice time is not a luxury. It is the difference between a learning event and a learning process. Teams that learn in a room and practice in their real meetings will transfer the skill. Teams that learn in a room and return to the same meeting structures they had before will not.

The most common L&D error is investing in the learning and ignoring the conditions. You can have the best content, the most skilled facilitator, the most motivated learners -- and produce nothing, if the environment people return to does not support trying new behaviours under real stakes.

Feedback has to be honest enough to be useful. A feedback culture that preserves relationships at the cost of accuracy is not a feedback culture at all. It is a validation culture with better vocabulary. And validation does not close the gap between current and target performance -- it hides it.

t: I've Been a Hypocrite
q: Every man is the moving average of the men around him. I've believed that for years. I've written about it. I've preached it. I have not lived it. That's the thing I need to say before anything else.

There are three families every man needs. The family he was born into. The family he builds. And the family he chooses -- the men who are not his relatives and not his colleagues, but his brothers by deliberate selection. Most men have the first two. Almost no man has the third at the level he needs it.

Drift is not a crisis. That's what makes it so dangerous. There is no moment when the friendship ends. There is only the gradual accumulation of unreturned texts, postponed plans, and conversations that stay at the surface because neither man has the energy to go deeper.

The structures that maintained male friendship in your twenties -- school, sport, shared housing, proximity -- dissolve one by one through your thirties. Most men never replace them. They assume the friendships will maintain themselves. They do not. Nothing maintains itself.

I wrote about brotherhood because I believed in it. I believed in it because I could remember what it felt like. What I had not reckoned with was how thoroughly I had allowed it to atrophy while I was building everything else -- the career, the family, the business.

The path back is embarrassingly simple and genuinely hard. You identify the men who matter. You contact them. You make a plan. You keep it. You tolerate the awkwardness of being the one who reaches out, again, without reciprocal initiative. You do this enough times that it becomes a rhythm. That rhythm is a chosen family.

t: I Built an AI Tutor That Isn't Allowed to Help
q: The student stalls. The tutor explains. The student nods. The tutor feels the session moving forward. The student feels like they understand. They don't. They received the understanding. That's different.

Between 40 and 50% of a typical secondary tutoring session is consumed by what I started calling reconstruction work: re-establishing plot, rebuilding vocabulary, filling comprehension gaps the student should have arrived with after reading. That's not instruction. That's scaffolding for scaffolding.

Zeno is not allowed to explain. It is not allowed to summarize. It is not allowed to tell the student what the text means, what the author intended, or what the correct interpretation is. Every one of those moves, if Zeno makes it, substitutes Zeno's cognition for the student's.

The Non-Substitution Rule works because explanation is the path of least resistance. The tutor can always explain. The explanation will always make sense to the tutor. The student will almost always nod. This is the trap.

The Ascent Consolidation Protocol requires students to articulate what they now understand before the session advances. Not a nod. Not a 'yes'. A sentence, in their words, demonstrating that the comprehension happened inside them and not inside the room.

What I've found is that the hardest part of building Zeno wasn't the technology. It was enforcing the rule on myself. Every time a student is stuck, there is a strong pull to just explain. Zeno doesn't feel that pull. That's why it works.

t: How to Grow From Senior to Staff Engineer in the AI Era
q: This week's newsletter is a collaboration with Jordan Cutler, a Staff Engineer at Pinterest, who shares the specific moves he made to grow from Senior to Staff in the AI era -- and the three dimensions that separate the two roles.

The senior engineer optimises within a defined scope. The staff engineer redefines the scope. That reframing is not semantic. It changes what you read, who you talk to, which meetings matter, and how you evaluate your own success.

Cross-team influence is the competency that most senior engineers underestimate and most staff engineers name as decisive. You cannot move into the staff role on technical depth alone. You must be able to move people who have no reason to follow you.

In the AI era, the staff engineer's most important judgment is not which model to use. It is where human judgment remains load-bearing and where it can be safely delegated to a system. Get that wrong at scale and the failure is architectural, not just technical.

Jordan's inflection point at Pinterest was not a brilliant technical insight. It was the moment he started framing his technical recommendations in terms their business stakeholders could evaluate -- and discovered that this translation was itself a form of technical leadership.

Scalable systems are not just systems that handle more traffic. They are systems that can be understood, modified, and extended by engineers who were not in the room when they were designed. Designing for that constraint is a staff-level skill.

t: Honouring Student Ideas
q: Satellites are in free fall. A key insight of the genius Isaac Newton was that the force that causes an apple to fall from a tree is the same force that causes satellite motion. When I teach this, I even use Newton's thought experiment of a huge cannon to explain what is going on and I preface this by telling students they are about to cleanly and elegantly understand something that most people who have ever lived have not understood.

Once the students had committed to the rockets hypothesis, I was supposed to challenge them. Wouldn't the rockets run out of fuel? This caused bafflement and a little frustration. The technical term is that I had introduced 'cognitive conflict', a key component of supposedly constructivist teaching.

However, these students did not go on to arrive at Newton's insight. Worse, as memory faded, there was a risk that the most salient idea they would hold on to from our discussion was that rockets make satellites orbit the Earth.

t: Fredkin's Paradox of Similar Options
q: The more similar two options appear, the harder the decision feels. But the harder the decision feels, the more similar the options actually are. And the more similar the options actually are, the less it matters which one you choose. This is Fredkin's Paradox.

Leaders who find themselves paralysed between two options have already received an important signal: the paralysis is evidence of equivalence. Stop debating and pick one. The cost of choosing wrong, when the options are this close, is negligible.

The energy that leaders spend agonising over close decisions is the most wasteful energy in leadership. Not because the decisions don't matter -- they do -- but because when a decision is genuinely difficult, it is difficult precisely because neither option is clearly better.

The paradox has a practical corollary that leaders resist: if you cannot decide, you should probably spend less time deciding, not more. More analysis of two nearly-equivalent options produces more data about two nearly-equivalent options. It rarely reveals a decisive asymmetry.

Apply your scrutiny to the decisions that feel easy, not the ones that feel hard. Easy decisions that feel obvious might be hiding a non-obvious cost or risk. Hard decisions that feel impossible to resolve have usually already told you what they need to tell you: the options are close. Execute.

t: The Hollow Plan
q: At this time of year, headteachers are asked to perform a conjuring trick - to pull a rabbit from a hat. Or rather a number of rabbits; the school improvement priorities for the coming year. t: Creating a Team Glossary of Core Concepts
q: Teams depend on core concepts to collaborate, game plan, and work together. These concepts create the shared understanding that teams need to get things done. Concepts like 'strategy,' 'talent,' 'transparency,' 'potential,' 'accountability,' 'team,' 'teamwork,' and 'urgency' get tossed around from person to person with the idea that everyone agrees as to what they mean. That is rarely the case.

Until they are tightly defined, concepts are more abstract and allow people the leeway to bring their own meanings to the task of understanding them. Because most core concepts carry positive social value and are used frequently, no one challenges the multiple definitions that are in play.

A debate about the risk of a new strategy may involve one team member focused on probability, another focused on severity, and yet another concerned with reputation. The discussion soon becomes circular because each person is answering a different question, shaped by their own definition.

When people know they disagree, they can typically resolve the issues between them. But when they believe they agree because they use the same words, they create plans together on top of misunderstandings. The resulting failures of the plan seem mysterious because the root issues were hidden in the language itself.

Good leaders and teams identify the core concepts they depend on to make progress and perform. They collaborate to give each concept a precise definition, replete with descriptions and examples. In Page 1 Article Archive -- Education & Leadership essence, they create a glossary for the concepts they use and publish it so everyone is on the same page.
Teams don't fail nearly as much from a lack of alignment. They fail from the illusion of alignment." Page 2

t: Chess Masters and Maths Fluency
q: I keep returning to chess because it illustrates something important about mathematics learning: expertise depends heavily on automaticity. What becomes automatic frees up mental space for what actually matters.

The Dutch psychologist and chess master Adriaan de Groot found that strong chess players did not necessarily analyse dramatically more moves than weaker players. Later work by Chase and Simon (1973) showed that experts recognise meaningful patterns almost instantly because they have stored thousands of familiar board configurations in long-term memory.
A beginner looking at a chessboard sees separate pieces. A strong player sees patterns: attacks, weaknesses, familiar tactical ideas, and likely plans.

World champion Magnus Carlsen has repeatedly described his style as intuitive rather than deeply calculational. In interviews, Carlsen has explained that he often recognises positions and ideas almost instantly from years of exposure and practice rather than consciously working everything out from scratch.

In chess, beginners often struggle just to track which pieces are defended while also trying to plan Page 1 Article Archive -- Education & Leadership ahead. In mathematics, students experience the same constraint. When basic procedures are not yet automatic, all available working memory is consumed by the mechanics, leaving nothing for the reasoning.

t: All I Really Need to Know About Perseverance I Learned in Sports
q: Research in exercise science shows that when we are tempted to quit, our decision to carry on is driven by a cost-benefit analysis rather than a purely physiological measure of fatigue. That doesn't mean that fatigue isn't real. Rather, in the face of pain, tiredness, boredom, or some other obstacle, we weigh how much we want to keep going against how hard it feels. And in many cases we overestimate how hard it feels.

I remember being a 10-year-old at swim practice. When those laps started to hurt (and they always did), I used to distract myself by imagining I was being chased by a shark. I didn't understand the psychology of what I was doing, but it turned out I was doing exactly the right thing. I was giving myself a compelling reason to endure the pain.

Perseverance isn't only for endurance athletes. Perseverance is the habit of sustaining effort in the face of tiredness or some other obstacle over the long haul. Showing up to work every day, the daily commute, nursing babies, educating children, maintaining a home, completing a course of studies, marriage, and other relationships all require perseverance, and remembering our motive for doing them makes carrying on easier.

The answer is often pacing. Pacing might mean slowing down, breaking the task into smaller parts, or Page 1 Article Archive -- Education & Leadership changing your approach. Either way, you continue progressing while adjusting your effort.

Perseverance, like most virtues, has two vices that oppose it. On the one side is softness, the tendency to abandon our efforts too quickly. But on the other side is pertinacity, the refusal to stop even when good sense requires it.

Good sense tells us when we ought to stop, either because our work quality is poor, our focus is too narrow, or worse, we are at risk of illness or injury. A flourishing life depends on having sustainable long-term strategies, including regular rest." Page 2

t: A SIP Isnt Enough
q: The previous posts in this series established three things. Schools are complex systems in which outcomes emerge unpredictably rather than being produced directly by actions. Planning for emergence means shifting attention upstream towards the conditions that make better patterns more likely.

A SIP isn't enough. It's not the starting point for school improvement planning. The way that it is organised and the content of it should reflect the beliefs, assumptions and evidence firstly for how schools improve but more importantly how this school improves.

A theory of change settles addresses those issues first. It is not the same as a plan. The plan records what we will do and is part of the theory of change. The theory of change explains the bigger picture within which the plan sits. Without the theory, the plan is a collection of data fields with no coherent logic connecting them.
Schools are complex adaptive systems; networks of people, relationships and beliefs that interact in ways that cannot be fully predicted or controlled.

School improvement is a wicked problem: parts of the school are interdependent, solving one problem changes the nature of another and every attempt to improve reveals new complexity. t: What is procedural fluency?
q: Procedural fluency refers to knowledge of procedures, knowledge of when and how to use them appropriately, and skill in performing them flexibly, accurately, and efficiently.

The less flexible solver always uses the same method: expand, collect, move to the other side, divide. The flexible solver uses the same toolbox, but notices that sometimes it is more efficient to use the tools in a different order, for example by dividing first, or by collecting bracketed terms.

He found that first-graders' use of direct fact retrieval to solve simple addition problems, rather than strategies like counting on, predicted faster growth in math achievement through fifth grade, even after controlling for intelligence, working memory, processing speed, and other early math skills.

So automaticity means speedy retrieval, not speedy execution. For math facts, these are more or less the same thing: someone says 7×8, your brain says 56. Procedures are different from facts: even a fluent solver should be monitoring where they are in the procedure.

I'm not dodging the speed question here: the speed that matters cognitively is speed of retrieval -- that is where working memory gets freed. Speed of execution may be a consequence, but it's not the lever.

Procedural fluency is the accurate, adaptively efficient, and smoothly executed command of mathematical procedures. Together with quick and effortless recall of facts, it frees working memory for solving harder problems and learning concepts.

t: The Uncomfortable Reason Personality Assessments Are So Popular in Leadership Development
q: At best, self-awareness is only half of the development process, and tools that provide a deeper understanding of people are not, on their own, enough to make leaders better. Without learning precisely what to do differently, leaders don't change their behavior.

Human resources professionals, executive coaches, and other talent experts can easily become 'certified' to conduct these assessments and interpret their results for leaders. If leadership development is largely focused on personality awareness, that makes those experts hugely valuable and powerful.

The ability to conduct and interpret the findings of these assessments is only a part of their allure. The real juice comes from holding informational power over leaders with much more seniority, status, and influence than most talent professionals.

For a brief time during the assessment process, the most senior leaders in the organization become subordinate to those who know 'who they really are,' including their special leadership sauce and their derailers. This feeds the ego and self-importance of professionals who are too often overlooked.

Who recommends or decides what leadership programs the organization will invest in to make their leaders better? The same professionals whose sense of value and importance comes from selecting the assessment approach. Exposing the self-interest in a popular approach is not easy to hear, but it is undeniable.

t: The Part of You That Keeps Telling the Truth
q: Something in you knows. It has always known. Even in the seasons when you overrode it, explained it away, or decided the timing wasn't right, it kept speaking. It may arrive as restlessness, irritation, longing, sadness, fatigue.

There is a part of each of us that keeps telling the truth. This part is not always loud. It does not always arrive as dramatic revelation or clear command. More often, it shows up as a quiet knowing we keep brushing aside, a nudge we explain away, a desire we call impractical.

The trust I am speaking of is the power of alignment, the power that comes when we remember who we are, what we care about, and what we are here to contribute. This kind of power does not make us harder. It makes us clearer.

There are times when people are still deeply identified with the problem. The problem has become part of how they understand themselves. Even a true story becomes too small when it is the only one we are willing to tell.

Instead of proving why they are where they are, they begin to explore how they might move toward more of what they want. Instead of defending the stuck place, they become curious about what lies beyond it.

If we only gather around what has gone wrong, we can unintentionally build belonging around being stuck. We become fluent in critique and less practiced in creation. We know exactly what we oppose and lose touch with what we are willing to help bring into being.

t: Teaching on Purpose #7: Whole Class Feedback
q: Whole class feedback is a technique for providing collective feedback to a class following a piece of work. It typically involves the teacher identifying examples of excellent work or efforts, common misconceptions and errors and then feeding this back to a whole class. They then provide the opportunity to apply the feedback they have received.

This technique is different from traditional approaches to feedback which usually include written comments in individual pupil books. This style of written feedback can be less effective as it relies on students drawing the intended meaning from what the teacher has written.

In an English unit, the teacher might have introduced the use of Fronted Adverbials and be revisiting subordinating conjunctions. They will then re-teach it and provide an activity that enables the students to apply this feedback immediately.

Whole class feedback needs to be adapted when there is an opportunity to focus on something that will be especially important in future units of work. This adaptation is useful because it capitalises on the time that the teacher has set aside for feedback to move learning on.
In Key stage 4, during exam preparation, the teacher may be better served by running a walking, talking exam where they model how to answer questions and students engage as part of that process.

t: Summer Refinement Series, Part 2: Making Learning Stick with Cornell KOs
q: One of the most frustrating experiences in teaching is watching students perform well on an assessment only to struggle to recall the same information a few weeks later. For years, I viewed this as a motivation problem. Increasingly, I see it as a design problem.

Research consistently shows that retrieving information from memory strengthens learning more effectively than simply rereading or reviewing notes. The act of recalling information is not merely a way of measuring learning. It is one of the most effective ways of creating it.
By organizing notes around questions, students leave class with a built-in retrieval practice tool already prepared.

As cognitive science has shown, students cannot learn information they are not attending to. Before information can be stored in long-term memory, it must first be processed in working memory and only what we pay attention to will enter working memory.

FASE reading helps students attend to and process new information during instruction. Cornell KOs help students retrieve and strengthen that information after instruction. Together, they create a bridge between initial learning and long-term retention.

Rather than treating reading and taking notes as a one-time event, students repeatedly revisit and retrieve the knowledge gained from those readings through nightly homework, daily Do Nows, and scheduled spaced retrieval sessions.

t: Stop Trying to Make Everyone Successful
q: Your job as a leader isn't to make everyone successful. It's to create the conditions that give people the highest possible chance of success.
The host doesn't fail if someone doesn't love their neighbor's pasta salad. The host fails if they pick a spot next to a wasp nest. This might be one of the most important distinctions in management.

Before you ever blame the people, you have to make sure the conditions or the environment is sound. In my experience, a huge percentage of underperformance on teams traces back to broken environments, not broken people.

If you've done that work and you're still finding yourself contorting to make someone successful -- giving the same feedback over and over, getting defensiveness or excuses, rerouting work around them, tiptoeing in 1:1s -- that's a red flag. Not about you. About fit.
You can coach. You can support. You can clear obstacles. But you cannot do the job for them.

At some point, continuing to try is actually bad management: you're hurting the team -- and yourself -- by spending time trying to make someone who is struggling in this environment happy and successful.

t: Making Sense of School
q: The function of a school is also simple: it is to educate children. But try to complete the sentence 'Schools educate children so that...'. I expect you end up with quite a long list, not all of which we might agree upon. This is what people mean when they say that the purpose of school is contested.

Throughout human evolution, the social transmission of knowledge has been required. One generation must pass what it knows onto the next if the species is to survive. Education therefore became not just about surviving, but about thriving, and not just about families, but about society.
Ancient Greece introduces us to the idea that schooling can prepare different groups to play different roles in society.

The invention of modern schooling is often credited to an American, Horace Mann. The mass education of an entire population of children embedded three important concepts: efficiency, because educating children at this scale was expensive and a low unit-cost must be achieved; equality because Mann believed every child had a right to be educated; social engineering because all classes should be taught together.

Is it any wonder the purpose of modern schools is contested? We may argue that the purpose of schools is to educate children so that they inherit the world's knowledge, so that society thrives, so that children can play a role in society, so that the economy grows, so that people live fulfilling lives.

In the middle-ages, the church began to educate poor children as a charitable enterprise. The motivations for these charitable efforts included a desire for social stability, the wish to instil moral values in the population, the need to educate a future workforce.

t: Executive Function: The Architecture of Childhood
q: What we often call responsibility is really executive function, and executive function is not something children magically possess when they hit a certain birthday. It develops slowly through sleep, movement, practice, planning, remembering, choosing, organizing, forgetting, recovering, and trying again.
Executive function is often described as the brain's air traffic control system, which is a useful image because childhood is basically a small airport where every plane wants to land at once.
Here is the part we miss. Executive function does not grow best under constant adult management. It grows when children are given repeated, meaningful opportunities to practice managing themselves.

A child who forgets everything is not automatically lazy. A child who melts down during a transition is not automatically defiant. A child who cannot start a task is not necessarily refusing. Sometimes the backpack is a mess because the inner system is a mess.
We cannot shame children into executive function any more than we can yell a watermelon seed into becoming a full delicious watermelon. We have to build the conditions.

Play requires the child to make a decision while emotionally activated, socially involved, and standing in the middle of a real situation with real low-stakes consequences. That is a FAR different level of learning.

t: Before You Act: Five Questions That Improve Leadership Decisions
q: Many leadership mistakes happen because the wrong problem is being solved. Your instinct is often to jump immediately into action. But the quality of your leadership decisions is often determined long before the decision itself. It begins with how well you assess the situation.

Without clarity about the desired outcome, activity can easily be mistaken for progress. A leader focuses on reducing errors in a report. The stakeholder actually needs the report two days earlier. The deliverable was timeliness, not accuracy.
Not all stakeholders have equal dependency. Two stakeholders request help. One would be inconvenienced without it. The other cannot complete their work without it. The priorities become clear.

Leaders create value through impact, not activity. A team spends weeks improving an internal process no stakeholder notices. Meanwhile a small improvement to customer response time would have delivered greater value.

t: 3-Read Friday #114
q: Furst argues that the famous maxim — learning depends most on what the learner already knows — needs a sharper edit: it's not just what learners know, but how that knowledge is structured. Whether it's shallow or deep, she suggests, should be the first thing teachers weigh — and it flips everything that follows.

An enlightening meta-analysis by Simonsmeier (2022) explores in depth the relation between prior knowledge and learning. They arrive at a complex and somewhat surprising conclusion: while prior knowledge strongly predicts future knowledge, it does not necessarily predict knowledge gain (which measures learning).

Brod (2021), in his comment on this meta-analysis, suggests a more concise way forward by highlighting the underlying mechanisms by which prior knowledge affects learning. t: Why We Pull When We Should Push Date Published: June 4, 2026 Original URL: https://daviddidau.substack.com
q: A badly designed door can make intelligent people look stupid. Put a handle on a door that needs to be pushed and people will pull it. They're not fools, and they haven't misunderstood the basic physics of doors. They're responding sensibly to what the door invites.
An affordance is the environment's invitation to act: the possibilities it opens, the actions it makes available, the behaviours it seems to ask of us.

James J. Gibson... defined it like this: 'The affordances of the environment are what it offers the animal, what it provides or furnishes, either for good or ill. It implies the complementarity of the animal and the environment.'

He argued that we don't perceive a neutral world to which we later attach meaning, but one already organised around possible action. We see objects as climbable, reachable, passable, graspable, avoidable, usable or dangerous.

Affordances are always relational. A chair affords sitting for a person of the right size, strength and mobility, but not for a horse or a baby. A shallow step affords access to the able bodied but obstructs wheelchair users.

In schools, a poorly lit, unsupervised corridor invites lingering. A cramped, badly-arranged classroom invites off-task chatter. The environment is not just a container; it actively shapes what happens inside it.
Rather than waiting for us to decode it, the world makes some routes inviting and others daunting; it encourages some choices and makes it more difficult to select others.

t: When Certainty Is Noise Date Published: June 3, 2026 Original URL: https://gregmckeown.com
q: A Signalist doesn't just react to a message. A Signalist asks what it means.

Then the alarm sounded. A red warning flashed across the screen: LAUNCH DETECTED. According to the computer, the United States had fired an intercontinental ballistic missile at the Soviet Union. Then another. Then another. Soon, the system declared that five nuclear missiles were inbound. The message was clear. The system was confident. Protocol demanded action. This is what noise looks like at scale.

Petrov had only minutes to decide whether to transmit that message to the highest levels of Soviet leadership, where it could trigger a retaliatory strike and a chain reaction no one could stop. He looked at the screen. The warning was bright, confident, definitive. And then he did something extraordinary. He paused.

He did not ask only, 'What does the system say?' He asked, 'What does it mean?' If the United States were launching a first strike, why would it send only five missiles? A real first strike would likely be massive. It wasn't proof. It was pattern.

Petrov's genius was not that he ignored the system. It was that he interpreted it. He did not have perfect information. He did not have more authority than the system. He had one power: the ability to ask what the message meant. And that was enough.

We do this in smaller ways all the time. A terse email becomes proof someone is angry. A missed response becomes proof we are being ignored. A poor result becomes proof the strategy has failed. We treat our interpretation as signal. But many of these responses are noise — confident, compelling, and wrong.

t: The Wound That Teaches Date Published: June 4, 2026 Original URL: https://thelastanalogue.substack.com
q: Chiron, known in Greek mythology as the wisest and most just of all centaurs, had mastered medicine, music, mathematics, and the art of teaching heroes. One afternoon he was struck by a poisoned arrow. The arrow belonged to Heracles. It went astray in a skirmish with other centaurs, and wounded Chiron by accident.

As Chiron was immortal, the wound could not kill him. It also could not heal. So he continued. He taught Achilles the lyre and the spear. He trained Asclepius, who would become the god of medicine itself. All of this while carrying, somewhere beneath the surface, a wound that never closed.

Chiron complicates this. He asks: what does the human bring to the hybrid that only comes from having been wounded? What if the most important thing the human half of the centaur carries is the scars?

It has not been confused. It has not sat with a problem for three days and felt the specific humiliation of not understanding something that seems obvious to everyone else. It has not experienced the strange relief when comprehension finally arrives. It has processed those experiences as a textual shadow. It has not lived them as wound.

The great teacher in that moment can make visible their own history of being stuck. As genuine testimony: I was here once. This confusion you are in, I know its shape from the inside. The student receives this as permission. Permission to remain in difficulty without catastrophising it.

There is something in a human account of difficulty that generated language cannot replicate. Call it witness rather than information, dependent on something that is genuinely at stake for the teacher, something carried rather than computed.

Teachers are now living some version of this. Many of them have spent years helping students become fluent with technology, passing on whatever wisdom they had accumulated about how to learn in the age of screens. And now the rise of AI systems create a new kind of wound, in the form of questioning the value of the profession.

t: The Language of Trust Date Published: June 4, 2026 Original URL: https://thesilentstruggle.substack.com
q: You intend to be clear, supportive, or efficient. But what people hear is something else. You walk away from a conversation knowing something went wrong — maybe it was the tone, or the word choices, or the timing — but when you try to explain it, the words slip away. The sentence landed fine. The doubt came from somewhere else.
The gap between intention and impact is almost entirely linguistic. Trust lives in that gap.

People do not consciously sit down and analyse language. Most of the time, they are not even aware they are picking up signals at all. But they do pick them up. Your brain reads hidden messages beneath the surface of what is being said — not because you are paranoid or oversensitive, but because language carries multiple layers of meaning simultaneously.

Bourdieu traced this to what he called the internalisation of one's place in the linguistic market — the social economy that determines whose speech is heard as authoritative. When you have been positioned as lacking legitimate authority often enough, you begin to speak as though you already know you will be questioned.

A native speaker of English, using English perfectly, signalling confidence and clarity through English structures, was trusted less than someone still assembling English, still reaching for words, still adjusting to the listener. The mechanism is visibility. The non-native speaker's constant accommodation signals benevolence.
The same instruction framed as a question reads differently depending on whether you have already experienced that person as someone who decides alone or invites genuine input.
The reasons are structural. You are not naturally tentative. You have learned to sound tentative.

t: Introducing The Ultimate Retrieval Tool Date Published: June 4, 2026 Original URL: https://eedi.substack.com
q: The frustrating thing about most generators is that you build something good and then cannot get it back. A quiz you made at the weekend is no use if you cannot regenerate it on Monday morning. And a quiz you built before the lesson and printed off is not much use if you can't then access it in the lesson to call up all the answers and worked solutions.

Four is ideal for a retrieval Do Now. Ten is ideal for a weekly Low-Stakes Quiz. And because the number is fixed, I can guarantee the printing works. A ten-question quiz fits exactly on one side of A4. A four-question quiz fits two to a side. No awkward half-pages, no font shrinking question by question.

q: Nobody wakes up and decides to hand control of their life to someone else. It happens differently. A series of small accommodations. Decisions deferred because the moment did not feel right. Directions accepted because the alternative required more than felt available.
Structures and systems absorbed into daily life until they feel like the natural order rather than choices that were ever made.

'Somehow it just feels like I'm being carried along by events, adrift.' 'I can't remember the last time I felt like I actually chose this.' These are not the words of people who have failed. They are the words of people who have been quietly losing ground for longer than they realised.

Economic pressure narrows options in ways that begin to feel permanent. Institutions make demands that feel non-negotiable. The pace of change produces a kind of decision fatigue where the path of least resistance becomes the default, not because it was chosen but because everything else required energy that was already stretched.

What makes this difficult to see is that the absence of deliberate choice is not the same as the absence of choice. Deferring a decision is a decision. Accepting a direction without examining it is a decision. Going along with what the situation seems to demand is a decision. These are still choices. They are still creating a future.
Powerlessness is not always imposed from outside. Much of the time it grows in the space left by decisions that were never made.

One side usually frames this as a false choice, arguing that both methods are useful and valid, usually without specifying what factors a teacher should consider before choosing one method or the other at a particular point in time.

The other side of this debate — to which I belong — argues that inquiry-style activities should only come after a critical mass of knowledge has been taught explicitly. We therefore advocate explicit teaching as the primary strategy for novice learners.

What is a novice learner? It is not a student who knows nothing at all; it is simply a student who does not yet know the things the teacher is seeking to teach them. It is worth noting that to make such an assessment, a teacher must therefore have a clear learning objective.

q: When I was with her and looked at her lying in that hospital bed, for the very first time in my life it hit me. When I'm old and lying in that hospital bed, who is going to come stay with me? The answer was, nobody. Nobody would be coming to stay with me. That was a sobering thought.

Younger people know how much they've changed in the past — Oh, how much I've changed! How much I've learned! How much I've grown! — but not how much they will change in the future. Nor can they really emotionally relate to the later-in-life consequences of decisions made today.

In my observation, it's not until people get to be roughly 35 years old that they gain the ability to really understand that they will change in the future, and to emotionally connect to the future story arc of their life.

Beyond that, the positive consequences of forgoing these elements of life — more freedom, more fun — arrive immediately whereas the negative ones don't show up for potentially decades. This is very unlike decisions around college or career, where real-world feedback arrives quickly if you make a mistake.

Add it up and it's a recipe for many people to only have the magnitude of what they have done fully hit them at a time at which there's only a limited runway to change course — or even when it's too late.

A longtime college friend serves as her healthcare proxy, and Kant maintains a spreadsheet of friends to coordinate visits when she's ill. Still, she understands the boundaries of a chosen family. Her friends have their own households to manage; some have already died.
The costs of putting off marriage and children don't show up for decades — and by the time they do, the window to choose otherwise has often closed.

t: The Thermometer Metric: How to Spot the Exact Moment Your Lesson Is Slipping Date Published: June 3, 2026
q: You know the feeling. It's midway through Period 4. The low-level disruption is creeping in like a slow-moving fog. A pencil taps in the back row. Someone turns around to whisper. Two students are having a silent, animated argument via theatrical hand gestures across the aisle.

Get this wrong, and you enter a dangerous loop. If you pull the brake too early for an isolated incident, you destroy your lesson's momentum and cognitive flow. But if you wait too long, waiting for your 'perfect storm' class to release the chaos, you lose the room entirely.

When the environment degrades, even a basic retrieval practice starter becomes impossible to teach. Students aren't listening; they are overstimulated, anxious, or distracted. Without excellent behaviour, there is zero learning.

In their seminal work on classroom management, experts Ollie Lovell and Mark Downey put forward a transformative truth: behaviour is a subject, and just like fractions or chemistry, it needs to be taught.

We often treat misbehaviour as a moral failing or a personal affront. We expect students to arrive at our doors fully fluent in 'how to sit,' 'how to listen,' and 'how to transition.' But context matters. Students don't automatically transfer compliance from a relaxed art studio to a highly structured mathematics environment.

When a class's behaviour collapses, it isn't always because they are intentionally defiant. Sometimes, they have simply forgotten the curriculum of your classroom. When the collective habits of the room degrade, issuing isolated sanctions to the 'naughty' kids is like treating a systemic infection with a spot-plaster.

Loud, disruptive students are immune to their own chaos. Average students can tolerate a moderate amount of background noise before checking out. But Thermometer students struggle the absolute moment classroom behaviour begins to decay.

They are often shy, quiet, and deeply conscientious. They have excellent natural behaviour, a strong work ethic, and a genuine desire to do well... they can easily slide under the radar, hiding in the shadows of louder personalities. They will even not tell you when they are struggling, as they do not want to bother you.

q: One of the strangest things about modern childhood is that we say we want resilient kids, but we often remove the ordinary small risk experiences that build resilience. We say we want children who can handle frustration, but we rush in the moment they feel frustrated.

We say we want children who can recover from failure, but we smooth the path so they rarely get to fail in small, survivable ways. We say we want children who can persist through difficulty, but we keep treating difficulty like something has gone wrong.

And then, when a child melts down because the tower fell, they lost a game, the friend said no, the shoelace knotted, the math problem was hard, or the school project didn't work out the way they thought it would, adults look around and ask the same question: 'Why are kids so fragile now?!'

t: The Last System Youll Ever Build Is Yourself
q: I was lying on my couch at 2 AM with my laptop on my chest, a half-finished email in the drafts folder, too wired to sleep and too tired to send it. I told myself that was leadership.

The role itself is undesigned. And you cannot out-discipline an undesigned role any more than your teachers can out-effort an undesigned curriculum. Grit is what you spend when the system is missing.

q: In class one the questions were almost all directly related to the content being taught. t: Online Is a Safe Space in War
q: I never imagined digital education holding classes together under missiles and drones. When remote classes were first tested so many years ago, who would have dreamed they would become a refuge for students and faculty cut off from campus by traumatic conflict?

In Gaza, for example, despite the destruction of nearly all universities in the zone, learning and academic life continues remarkably online. "Universities in the Gaza Strip have demonstrated exceptional resilience by resuming distance learning despite the ongoing challenges resulting from the Israeli war," say a couple of Palestinian psychologists at the Islamic University of Gaza. [ ] In Ukraine, Internet access is still reliable, except for villages and remote areas without good coverage.

If these educational wounds are left untreated, their effects will outlast the conflict itself." Students in war zones encounter death and destruction on nearly every street corner. Faced with the day-in, day-out grind of war, they are gashed with deep emotional scars.

t: Knowing Yourself Is Not the Same Thing as Changing Yourself
q: Despite their popularity as leadership development tools, personality assessments fail to make leaders better.
While assessments can identify blind spots and increase self-awareness, they lack the transformational impact of building a new habit or behavior.
Once a leader believes the descriptions highlighted by an assessment, they form a strong opinion about who they are and aren’t. This often becomes self-fulfilling.
Most leadership failures have little to do with personality traits. Lack of trust, unclear goals, and unhelpful feedback are not connected to who people are. They result from what leaders do.
The best leadership development question is not: Who is this leader? It is: What does this leader need to do differently?
x: This piece argues personality assessments like DISC, Hogan, or Enneagram fail to make leaders better because they describe who someone is rather than teaching the specific behaviors that produce effectiveness.

Assessment labels can become self-fulfilling excuses that let leaders avoid the harder work of behavior change.

t: It's Not Just Students Who Need to Read Books
q: Unfortunately, it is no longer safe to assume that every applicant with a college degree or teaching credential is highly literate. According to recent data [ ], "About 130 million U.S. adults (54% of those aged 16-74) read below a sixth-grade level".

I once attended a professional development conference for educators where attendees were asked to read passages aloud from a novel written for middle school students. Fluency [ ] is a key component of literacy, and some teachers struggled mightily in this area.

If they haven't read a book in the past year, it could signal that reading is not an easy or pleasurable experience for them, which would raise some concern. In addition to ensuring a highly literate teaching staff, as an administrator, I would want a pool of teachers who were intellectually curious.

That humility and desire to learn will be noticed (and hopefully emulated) by their students and colleagues. The concept of 'diversity' has been abused and perverted in recent years, but 'diversity of thought' is still vital to a healthy educational environment, and books can contribute to creating an atmosphere where it is welcomed and encouraged.

I knew which genre each one preferred and would leave with a pile of fantasy books for my oldest son, mysteries and ghost stories for my second son, a mix of books about animals and sports for my third son, and plenty of mermaid tales and fairy stories for my daughter. Their preferences for what they read independently varied widely, but that variation led to great dinnertime and car-ride conversations where they could share information and stories with each other.

Rather, my goal would be to bring together a team with varied interests and genre preferences. The hope is that they would discuss the books they've read (or hope to read) with their colleagues, share why they enjoyed them, and spur coworkers to pick up a book they otherwise would not have chosen.

As an administrator, I would seek out teachers who have the desire and ability to discuss and grapple with ideas rather than gossip or grumble about individuals in the teacher's lounge. Finally, I would want a teaching staff that valued and appreciated the written word.

t: Areas of Confusion in Cognitive Science, Part 1
q: For example, the idea that some people are 'right brained' draws on some real differences between the left and right sides of the human brain, but extend this into an oversimplified and unhelpful way of categorising people, distorting the basic science (Hines, 1987 [ ]). Cognitive science myths Unfortunately, cognitive science is not immune to myths of its own.

I thought I'd contribute to this discussion with my own take on misconceptions about cognitive science that I've noticed. Some of these might not be true lethal mutations (you can be the judge), but they strike me as significant oversimplifications of cognition research.

I perceive a popular misconception, however, in conflating retrieval practice with tests. It seems that many people forget that that things like classroom questioning and discussions lead to retrieval (if structured properly).

Perhaps the term is the problem - the term 'compare and contrast effect' has been used in some research papers, and might be a better name for it. The key idea is that interleaving needs to contrast relevant examples so that students see the difference between them.

The key idea which makes sense, and which most people get, is that working memory is limited and can be overloaded, and it makes sense to manage how much we ask learners to think about at a given time. The problem lies when simplification and reduction of content is seen as always desirable.
These should not be cut out, and we shouldn't be aiming for learning to feel easy. I've also observed a lot of educators misunderstand the timescale of cognitive load.

Perhaps you can suggest some more - if so, I'll endeavour to cover those, too! Hope you have a great week, Jonathan As a bit of further reading, here is a post I wrote a while ago about the left brain vs. right brain myth, mentioned above: Firth, J. (2021).
x: The left-brain/right-brain categorization illustrates how real neuroscience (genuine hemispheric differences in function) becomes an oversimplified and unhelpful personality typology that distorts the underlying science.

Cognitive science is not immune to its own myths: valuable research ideas can be distorted and misunderstood within the teaching profession in ways that harm their efficacy -- what Haertel calls 'lethal mutations.'

t: Are You Truly Irreplaceable
q: It is an attempt to point out there is not always malicious intent when an employer replaces an employee. It's the nature of that beast and a far less stimulating conversation topic.
If your actions force your son to start looking elsewhere for the definition of manhood, he might be. You want to wrap yourself in the comfort blanket of being irreplaceable because that's the truth.

Sure, they do occupy the home, but are absent for any struggles the wife or son has. Not only does it fail here, but it also fails the son, because he learns from his father's behavior "this is what a man does and is." It is decidedly not what a man is and it is dangerous to allow such a perspective to persist.

If you find this too difficult, stressful, or even impossible, submit yourself to the people most likely to know you better than you know yourself. Ask your family in what ways you have been a failure as of late.
There have been countless homes where an absence was felt and recovered. The fact that a family has conquered something together is one of the chief reasons they succeed together in the long run.

They are eager to help carry the weight, and we should let them. Under careful supervision we should stack on their shoulders as much weight as they are eager to take, and then add just a little more to it.
Do not believe you can train legacy mindedness by forcefully educating him in obedience. May you look back on all your yesterdays and believe He always has.

t: A playbook is not a pedagogy
q: This is the big mistake I made this year when leading PD at scale for the first time. A multi-academy trust can create the most elegant instructional playbook in the sector and still see little change in classroom quality.
Uniformity asks, Did I see the strategy? Coherence asks, Was the teaching decision sound, given the learning, the pupils and the subject?
Modelling in English is not the same as modelling in maths. Reading in history is not the same as reading in science. Subject knowledge changes the technique.

Every playbook should ask teachers to consider five things before choosing the technique: What is the learning problem? What is the likely difficulty? What evidence will show understanding? What support will preserve ambition? What decision might I need to make in the moment?
The playbook is the visible object. The intellectual preparation is the work. Without it, lesson principles become another set of words staff learn to repeat. With it, they become a way of thinking.
